nodes.label: bottleneck traveling salesman
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bottleneck traveling salesman as: Find a tour where no edge is more costly than some (bottleneck) amount.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bottleneckTravelingSales

nodes.label: boundary-based representation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines boundary-based representation as: A representation of a region that is based on its boundary.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boundarybasd

nodes.label: bounded queue
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bounded queue as: A queue limited to a fixed number of items.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boundedqueue

nodes.label: bounded stack
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bounded stack as: A stack limited to a fixed number of items.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boundedstack

nodes.label: Boyer-Moore-Horspool
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Boyer-Moore-Horspool as: A string matching algorithm that compares characters from the end of the pattern to its beginning. When characters don't match, searching jumps to the next matching position in the pattern. Also known as Horspool.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boyerMooreHorspool

nodes.label: bozo sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bozo sort as: A terribly inefficient sort algorithm that randomly swaps items until they are in order.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bozoSort

nodes.label: BPP
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BPP as: The class of languages for which a membership computation by a probabilistic Turing machine halts in polynomial time with the right answer (accept or reject) at least 2/3 of the time. "BPP" means " B ounded error P robability in P olynomial" time. Also known as bounded error probability in polynomial time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bpp

nodes.label: Bradford's law
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Bradford's law as: Journals in a field can be divided into three parts, each with about one-third of all articles: 1) a core of a few journals, 2) a second zone, with more journals, and 3) a third zone, with the bulk of journals. The number of journals is 1:n:n².

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bradfordsLaw

nodes.label: Bresenham's algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Bresenham's algorithm as: An efficient algorithm to render a line with pixels. The long dimension is incremented for each pixel, and the fractional slope is accumulated.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bresenham

nodes.label: bridge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bridge as: An edge of a connected graph whose removal would make the graph unconnected.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bridge

nodes.label: British Museum technique
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines British Museum technique as: Find a solution by checking all possibilities one by one, beginning with the smallest. This is a conceptual, not a practical, technique where the number of possibilities are enormous.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: britishMuseum

nodes.label: brute force string search with mismatches
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines brute force string search with mismatches as: Beginning with the (leftmost) position in a string and trying each position in turn, find the number of characters for which the pattern and the substring beginning at that position don't match (the Hamming distance ). Return the first position with k or fewer mismatches.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bruteForceStrSrchwMismatch

nodes.label: brute force string search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines brute force string search as: Find a string in another string or body of text by trying each position one at a time. There are many far faster string matching algorithms. Also known as naive string search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bruteForceStringSearch

nodes.label: brute force
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines brute force as: An algorithm that inefficiently solves a problem, often by trying every one of a wide range of possible solutions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bruteforce

nodes.label: BSP-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BSP-tree as: A binary space partitioning (BSP) tree is a binary tree for multidimensional points where successive levels are split by arbitrary hyperplanes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bsptree

nodes.label: B*-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines B*-tree as: A B-tree in which nodes are kept 2/3 full by redistributing keys to fill two child nodes, then splitting them into three nodes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bstartree

nodes.label: bucket
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bucket as: An area of storage where items with a common property are stored. Typically tree data structures and sort algorithms use many buckets, one for each group of items. Usually buckets are kept on disk.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bucket

nodes.label: bucket trie
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bucket trie as: A variant of a trie in which leaf nodes are buckets which hold up to k strings. Usually implies fixed sized buckets.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bucketTrie

nodes.label: bucketing method
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines bucketing method as: Data organization methods that decompose the space from which spatial data is drawn into regions called buckets. Some conditions for the choice of region boundaries include the number of objects that they contain or on their spatial layout (e.g. minimizing overlap or coverage).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bucketmeth

nodes.label: buddy system
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines buddy system as: A memory allocation strategy which recursively divides allocatable blocks of memory into pairs of adjacent equal-sized blocks called "buddies".

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: buddysystem

nodes.label: buddy tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines buddy tree as: A point access method which splits multidimensional space in different dimensions at each level. It also keeps a minimum bounding box of points accessible by each node.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: buddytree

nodes.label: build-heap
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines build-heap as: Convert an array into a heap by executing heapify progressively closer to the root . For an array of n nodes, this takes O(n) time under the comparison model.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: buildHeap

nodes.label: Burrows-Wheeler transform
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Burrows-Wheeler transform as: Permute a string . Repeated substrings lead to repeated characters in the permuted string, which is easier to compress. Knowing which character was last in the original string, the original can be reconstructed from the rearranged string. Also known as BWT.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: burrowsWheelerTransform

nodes.label: busy beaver
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines busy beaver as: (1) A Turing machine with a small number of states that halts when started with a blank tape, but writes a huge number of non-blanks or takes a huge number of steps. (2) The problem of finding the maximum number of non-blanks written or steps taken for any Turing machines with a given number of states and symbols.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: busyBeaver

nodes.label: BV-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines BV-tree as: A conceptual idea which generalizes B-trees to multiple dimensions. BV-trees are not balanced, and searching may require backtracking .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bvtree

nodes.label: Byzantine generals
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Byzantine generals as: The problem of reaching a consensus among distributed units if some of them give misleading answers. To be memorable, the problem is couched in terms of generals deciding on a common plan of attack. Some traitorous generals may lie about whether they will support a particular plan and what other generals told them. Exchanging only messages, what decision making algorithm should the generals use to reach a consensus? What percentage of liars can the algorithm tolerate and still correctly determine a consensus?

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: byzantine

nodes.label: cactus stack
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cactus stack as: A variant of stack in which one other cactus stack may be attached to the top. An attached stack is called a "branch." When a branch becomes empty, it is removed. Pop is not allowed if there is a branch. A branch is only accessible through the original reference; it is not accessible through the stack. Formal Definition: The operations new to this variant of stack, branch(S, T) and notch(v), may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. top(branch(S, T)) = top(S) notch(new()) = false notch(push(v, S)) = false notch(branch(S, T)) = true Also known as saguaro stack.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cactusstack

nodes.label: Calculus of Communicating Systems
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Calculus of Communicating Systems as: Robin Milner's algebraic theory to formalize the notion of concurrent computation. Commonly known as CCS.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: calcucommsys

nodes.label: calendar queue
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines calendar queue as: A fast priority queue implementation having N buckets each with width w, or covering w time. An item with priority p more than current goes in bucket (p/w)%N. Choose N and w to have few items in each bucket. Keep items sorted within buckets. Double or halve N and change w if the number of items grows or shrinks a lot.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: calendarQueue

nodes.label: candidate consistency testing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines candidate consistency testing as: The stage of two-dimensional matching where a candidate occurrence of the pattern is checked against the "witness" table.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: candidate

nodes.label: candidate verification
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines candidate verification as: The stage of two-dimensional matching where candidate occurrences of the pattern are actually tested.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: candidateVerification

nodes.label: canonical complexity class
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines canonical complexity class as: One of the classes defined by logarithmic , polynomial , and exponential bounds on time and space, for deterministic and nondeterministic machines. These classify most of the important computational problems.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: canonical

nodes.label: capacitated facility location
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines capacitated facility location as: Given a set of demand points, a distance function, and a parameter p, find a set of p supply object (points, lines, segments, etc.) which minimizes some distance objective function and no supply supports too many demand points.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: capacifacloc

nodes.label: capacity
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines capacity as: The maximum flow that may be sent through an edge or a vertex .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: capacity

nodes.label: capacity constraint
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines capacity constraint as: The property that the flow on every edge of a flow network is no more than the edge's capacity . More formally, for all edges e, f(e) ≤ u(e), where f(e) is the flow on e and u(e) is its capacity.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: capacitycstr

nodes.label: Caverphone
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Caverphone as: An algorithm to code English names phonetically.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: caverphone

nodes.label: CCS
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines CCS as: Robin Milner's algebraic theory to formalize the notion of concurrent computation. An acronym for Calculus of Communicating Systems.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ccs

nodes.label: cell probe model
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cell probe model as: A model of computation where the cost of a computation is measured by the total number of memory accesses to a random access memory with ⌈log n⌉ bits cell size. All other computations are not counted and are considered to be free.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cellProbeModel

nodes.label: cell tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cell tree as: A spatial access method where successive levels are split by arbitrary hyperplanes. Concave objects are decomposed into convex pieces. Each convex piece is indexed in every cell which it overlaps.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: celltree

nodes.label: cellular automaton
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cellular automaton as: Usually a two-dimensional organization of simple finite state machines whose next state depends on their own state and the states of their eight closest neighbors. In general the machines may be arranged in meshes of higher or lower dimension, have larger neighborhoods, or be arbitrarily complex processors.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cellulartmtn

nodes.label: centroid
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines centroid as: The center of gravity or center of mass of an object.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: centroid

nodes.label: certificate
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines certificate as: (1) Extra information so the correctness of an answer to a decision problem can be quickly checked. (2) For any graph property P and graph G, a certificate for G is a graph G' such that G has property P if and only if G' has the property.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: certificate

nodes.label: chain
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines chain as: A set with a total order .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chain

nodes.label: chaining
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines chaining as: A class of collision resolution schemes in which linked lists handle collisions in a hash table . The two main subclasses are separate chaining , where lists are outside the table, and coalesced chaining , where the lists are within the table.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chaining

nodes.label: child
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines child as: A node of a tree referred to by a parent node. See the figure at tree . Every node, except the root , is the child of some parent.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: child

nodes.label: Chinese postman problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Chinese postman problem as: Find a minimum length closed walk that traverses each edge at least once. Finding an optimal solution in a graph with both directed and undirected edges is NP-complete .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chinesePostman

nodes.label: Chinese remainder theorem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Chinese remainder theorem as: An integer n can be solved uniquely mod LCM(A(i)) , given modulii (n mod A(i)), A(i) > 0 for i=1..k, k > 0. In other words, given the remainders an integer gets when it's divided by an arbitrary set of divisors, you can uniquely determine the integer's remainder when it is divided by the least common multiple of those divisors.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chineseRmndr

nodes.label: Christofides algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Christofides algorithm as: (1) A heuristic algorithm to find a near-optimal solution to the traveling salesman problem. Step 1: find a minimum spanning tree T. Step 2: find a perfect matching M among vertices with odd degree . Step 3: combine the edges of M and T to make a multigraph G. Step 4: find an Euler cycle in G. Step 5: Turn the Euler cycle into a Hamiltonian cycle by skipping vertices already seen. (2) An algorithm to find the chromatic number of a graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: christofides

nodes.label: chromatic number
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines chromatic number as: The minimum number of colors needed to color the vertices of a graph such that no two adjacent vertices have the same color.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chromatcnmbr

nodes.label: chromatic index
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines chromatic index as: The minimum number of colors needed to color the edges of a graph .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: chromaticndx

nodes.label: circuit
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines circuit as: (1) An acyclic network of inputs, logic gates, and outputs. Contrasted with a Turing machine , it has no memory. (2) A cycle in a graph .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: circuit

nodes.label: circuit complexity
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines circuit complexity as: The study of the size, depth, and other attributes of circuits that decide specified languages or compute specified functions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: circuitComplexity

nodes.label: clique
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines clique as: A set of vertices in an undirected graph in which there is an edge between every pair of vertices. In other words, a subgraph that is complete .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: clique

nodes.label: clique problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines clique problem as: Find the largest clique in an undirected graph .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cliqueproblm

nodes.label: clustering
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines clustering as: The tendency for entries in a hash table using open addressing to be stored together, even when the table has ample empty space to spread them out.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: clustering

nodes.label: clustering free
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines clustering free as: When a collision resolution scheme spreads out entries in a hash table .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: clusteringFree

nodes.label: coalesced chaining
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines coalesced chaining as: A scheme in which linked lists within the hash table handle collisions . An item that collides is put in the next empty place in the array and added to the end of a list embedded in the array items. Any open addressing method to compute possible new positions may be used to find the "next" empty place.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: coalescedChaining

nodes.label: coarsening
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines coarsening as: To alter a problem, typically restricting it to a less complex feasible region or objective function , so that the resulting problem can be efficiently solved, usually by dynamic programming .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: coarsening

nodes.label: codeword
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines codeword as: Sequence of bits of a code corresponding to a symbol.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: codeword

nodes.label: coding tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines coding tree as: A full binary tree that represents a coding, such as produced by Huffman coding . Each leaf is an encoded symbol. The path from the root to a leaf is its codeword.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: codingTree

nodes.label: collective recursion
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines collective recursion as: A special form of tail recursion , where the results are produced during the recursive calls and nothing is returned. The recursion may be optimized away by executing the call in the current stack frame, rather than creating a new stack frame, or by deallocating the entire recursion stack at once rather than a little at each return.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: collectiveRecursion

nodes.label: collision
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines collision as: When two or more items should be kept in the same location, especially in hash tables , that is, when two or more different keys hash to the same value.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: collision

nodes.label: collision resolution scheme
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines collision resolution scheme as: A way of handling collisions , that is, when two or more items should be kept in the same location, especially in a hash table . The general ways are keeping subsequent items within the table and computing possible locations ( open addressing ), keeping lists for items that collide ( chaining ), or keeping one special overflow area.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: collisionres

nodes.label: combination
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines combination as: Choose m of n elements, where m ≤ n.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: combination

nodes.label: Communicating Sequential Processes
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Communicating Sequential Processes as: C. A. R. Hoare's algebraic theory to formalize the notion of concurrent computation. Commonly known as CSP.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: communseqpro

nodes.label: commutative
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines commutative as: A function where f(A, B) = f(B, A).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: commutative

nodes.label: compact DAWG
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines compact DAWG as: A directed acyclic word graph (DAWG) representing the suffixes of a given string in which each edge is labeled with the longest possible string. The strings along a path from the root to a node are the substring which the node represents.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: compactDAWG

nodes.label: compact data structure
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines compact data structure as: A data structure that needs far less space and allows efficient access without decompression.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: compactDataStruct

nodes.label: compact trie
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines compact trie as: A trie in which nonbranching subtrees leading to leaf nodes are cut off.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: compactTrie

nodes.label: competitive analysis
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines competitive analysis as: An analysis in which the performance of an on-line algorithm is compared to the best that could have been achieved if all the inputs had been known in advance.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: competitiveAnalysis

nodes.label: competitive ratio
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines competitive ratio as: The worst case of the ratio between the cost incurred by an on-line algorithm and the best-case cost .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: competitivrt

nodes.label: complement
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complement as: (1) Of a boolean , 0 if 1, or 1 if 0. See not . (2) Of a set A, a set having all the members which are in the universe , but not in A.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: complement

nodes.label: complete binary tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complete binary tree as: A binary tree in which every level (depth), except possibly the deepest, is completely filled. At depth n, the height of the tree, all nodes must be as far left as possible.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: completeBinaryTree

nodes.label: complete tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complete tree as: A tree in which every level , except possibly the deepest, is entirely filled. At depth n, the height of the tree, all nodes are as far left as possible.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: completetree

nodes.label: complexity
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complexity as: The intrinsic minimum amount of resources, for instance, memory, time, messages, etc., needed to solve a problem or execute an algorithm .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: complexity

nodes.label: complexity class
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines complexity class as: Any of a set of computational problems with the same bounds ( Θ(n) ) on time and space, for deterministic and nondeterministic machines.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: complexityClass

nodes.label: compound algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines compound algorithm as: An algorithm in which one or more of the computable steps is a call to execute another algorithm.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: compoundAlgorithm

nodes.label: computable
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines computable as: A function that can be computed by an algorithm --- equivalently, by a Turing machine .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: computable

nodes.label: concurrent data structure
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines concurrent data structure as: A data structure designed to work correctly while being accessed by many asynchronous threads. The two main types are blocking and nonblocking.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: concurrentDataStructure

nodes.label: concurrent read, concurrent write
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines concurrent read, concurrent write as: A parallel memory model in which multiple processors can read simultaneously from a single memory location, and multiple processors can write simultaneously to a single memory location. Also known as CRCW.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: concurrentReadConWrt

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines concurrent read, exclusive write as: A parallel memory model in which multiple processors can read simultaneously from a single memory location, but only one processor can write to any one memory location at one time. Also known as CREW.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: concurrentReadExcluWrt

nodes.label: concurrent flow
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines concurrent flow as: A multi-commodity flow in which the same fraction of the demand of each commodity is satisfied.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: concurrntflw

nodes.label: confluently persistent data structure
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines confluently persistent data structure as: A fully persistent data structure that allows meld or merge operations to combine two different versions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: confluentlyPersistData

nodes.label: conjunction
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines conjunction as: The boolean and function.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: conjunction

nodes.label: connected components
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines connected components as: The set of maximally connected components of an undirected graph .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: connectedComponents

nodes.label: constant function
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines constant function as: A function that always gives the same value.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: constantfunc

nodes.label: Cook reduction
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Cook reduction as: A reduction computed by a deterministic polynomial time oracle Turing machine .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cookreductin

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Cook's theorem as: The language SAT of satisfiable Boolean formulas is NP-complete .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cookstheorem

nodes.label: CORDIC
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines CORDIC as: Compute trigonometric functions by iterative complex rotations. The advantage is that all computations can be done with addition, subtraction, and binary shifts.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cordic

nodes.label: covering
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines covering as: Given a finite collection of subsets of a finite ground set, to find an optimal subcollection whose union covers the ground set.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: covering

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines critical path problem as: Find the longest path from any source to any sinks in a directed acyclic graph which has weights, or numeric values, on vertices .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: criticalPath

nodes.label: CSP
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines CSP as: C. A. R. Hoare's algebraic theory to formalize the notion of concurrent computation. An acronym for Communicating Sequential Processes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: csp

nodes.label: CTL
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines CTL as: A propositional, branching-time temporal logic for which formulas can be checked in linear time. An acronym for Computation Tree Logic.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ctl

nodes.label: cut
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cut as: A nonempty, proper subset of vertices of a graph .

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cutting plane as: A valid inequality for an integer polyhedron that separates the polyhedron from a given point outside it.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines cut vertex as: A vertex whose deletion along with incident edges results in a graph with more components than the original graph. Also known as articulation point.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cutvertex

(2) An algorithm to compute bits characteristic of a block based on the algebra of polynomials over the integers, modulo 2. (3) The characteristic bits of a block. Also known as CRC.

nodes.label: Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm as: A quantum algorithm to determine whether a function is constant or balanced, that is, returns 1 for half the domain and 0 for the other half. For a function taking n input qubits, first, do Hadamards on n 0's, forming all possible inputs, and a single 1, which will be the answer qubit. Next, run the function once; this exclusive or 's the result with the answer qubit. Finally, do Hadamards on the n inputs again, and measure the answer qubit. If it is 0, the function is constant, otherwise the function is balanced.

nodes.label: dictionary
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines dictionary as: An abstract data type storing items, or values. A value is accessed by an associated key . Basic operations are new, insert, find and delete. Formal Definition: The operations new(), insert(k, v, D), and find(k, D) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a dictionary find(k, insert(k, v, D)) = v find(k, insert(j, v, D)) = find(k, D) if k ≠ j where k and j are keys, v is a value, and D is a dictionary. The modifier function delete(k, D) may be defined as follows. delete(k, new()) = new() delete(k, insert(k, v, D)) = delete(k, D) delete(k, insert(j, v, D)) = insert(j, v, delete(k, D)) if k ≠ j If we want find to be a total function , we could define find(k, new()) using a special value: fail . This only changes the return type of find. find(k, new()) = fail Also known as association list, map, property list.

Each set is every i th item, e.g. set 1 is item 1, 1+i, 1+2i, etc., set 2 is item 2, 2+i, etc. On each succeeding pass, the increment or gap, i, is reduced until it is 1 for the last pass.

nodes.label: distributive partitioning sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines distributive partitioning sort as: Step 1: find the median key . Step 3: compact the buckets, removing empty buckets. Recursively start again at step 1 for any bucket with multiple items. Linked lists are used to avoid moving items until a final phase and to avoid bucket overflows.

nodes.label: external quicksort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines external quicksort as: Read the M/2 first and last elements into a buffer (the buffer acts like the pivot in quicksort ), and sort them. Read the next element from the beginning or end to balance writing. If the next element is less than the least of the buffer, write it to available space at the beginning. If greater than the greatest, write it to the end. Otherwise write the greatest or least of the buffer, and put the next element in the buffer. Keep the maximum lower and minimum upper keys written to avoid resorting middle elements that are in order. When done, write the buffer. Recursively sort the smaller partition, and loop to sort the remaining partition.

nodes.label: fractional knapsack problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fractional knapsack problem as: Given materials of different values per unit volume and maximum amounts, find the most valuable mix of materials which fit in a knapsack of fixed volume. Since we may take pieces (fractions) of materials, a greedy algorithm finds the optimum. Take as much as possible of the material that is most valuable per unit volume. If there is still room, take as much as possible of the next most valuable material. Continue until the knapsack is full. Also known as continuous knapsack problem.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines free vertex as: A vertex not on a matched edge in a matching , or, one which has not been matched.

nodes.label: full binary tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines full binary tree as: A binary tree in which each node has exactly zero or two children . Also known as proper binary tree.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fully persistent data structure as: A persistent data structure that allows updates to all versions, previous and latest.

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fully dynamic graph problem as: Problem where the update operations include unrestricted insertions and deletions of edges .

nodes.label: fully polynomial approximation scheme
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines fully polynomial approximation scheme as: A set of algorithms {A ε | ε > 0}, where each A ε is a 1+ε- approximation algorithm bounded by a polynomial in the length of the input and 1/ε.

nodes.label: function
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines function as: (1) A computation which takes some arguments or inputs and yields an output. Any particular input yields the same output every time. More formally, a mapping from each element in the domain to an element in the range . (2) A subroutine which returns a value.

nodes.label: geometric optimization problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines geometric optimization problem as: An optimization problem induced by a collection of geometric objects.

nodes.label: global optimum
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines global optimum as: The best possible solution to a problem.

nodes.label: graph partition
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines graph partition as: Partition the vertices while keeping the cost of spanning edges low.

nodes.label: graph concentration
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines graph concentration as: Contracting a graph by removing a subset of the vertices .

nodes.label: graph drawing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines graph drawing as: The problem of representing a graph in a plane "neatly," for instance with a minimum number of edge crossings .

nodes.label: graph isomorphism
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines graph isomorphism as: Determine if two graphs are isomorphic .

nodes.label: greatest common divisor
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines greatest common divisor as: (1) The greatest integer which is a divisor of given positive integers. For instance, GCD(30, 42) = 6. (2) An algorithm to find the same. Also known as GCD, highest common factor.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: greatestCommonDivisor

nodes.label: greedy heuristic
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines greedy heuristic as: Solve an optimization problem by finding locally optimal solutions .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: greedyHeuristic

nodes.label: grid drawing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines grid drawing as: A graph drawing in which each vertex is represented by a point with integer coordinates.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: griddrawing

nodes.label: grid file
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines grid file as: A point access method which splits space into a nonperiodic grid. Each spatial dimension is divided by a linear hash . Small sets of points are referred to by one or more cells of the grid.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: gridfile

nodes.label: halting problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines halting problem as: Is there an algorithm to determine whether any arbitrary program halts? Turing proved the answer is, no. Since many questions can be recast to this problem, we can conclude that some programs are absolutely impossible, although heuristic or partial solutions are possible.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: haltingProblem

nodes.label: Hamiltonian cycle
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Hamiltonian cycle as: A path through a graph that starts and ends at the same vertex and includes every other vertex exactly once. Also known as tour.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hamiltonianCycle

nodes.label: Hamiltonian path
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Hamiltonian path as: A simple path through a graph that includes every vertex in the graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hamiltonianPath

nodes.label: hard split, easy merge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hard split, easy merge as: A recursive algorithm, especially a sort algorithm, where dividing (splitting) into smaller problems is time consuming or complex and combining (merging) the solutions is quick or trivial.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hardSplitEasyMerge

nodes.label: hashbelt
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hashbelt as: Use a short list or array of hash tables to implement a hash table with aging to expire items. To expire items, add a new table at the head of the list and drop the oldest table, along with its contents. To find an item, search all the tables.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hashbelt

nodes.label: hash heap
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hash heap as: An efficient implementation of a priority queue . The linear hash function monotonically maps keys to buckets , and each bucket is a heap .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hashheap

nodes.label: hash table delete
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hash table delete as: If the hash table uses chaining , use the chaining data structure delete. If it uses open addressing , mark the item "deleted" for future reuse.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hashtabdelet

nodes.label: Hausdorff distance
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Hausdorff distance as: A measure of the resemblance of two (fixed) sets of geometric points P and Q, defined as H(P,Q)=max{max a∈ P min b∈ Q d(a,b), max a∈ Q min b∈ P d(a,b)} where d(·,·) is the distance metric, usually the Euclidean distance .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hausdorffdst

nodes.label: hB-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hB-tree as: A point access method which uses k-d trees to organize the space, but partitions as excluded intervals, like the BANG file . Searching is like in a k-d-B-tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hbtree

nodes.label: head
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines head as: The first item of a list .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: head

nodes.label: heapify
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines heapify as: Rearrange a heap to maintain the heap property , that is, the key of the root node is more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the keys of its children . If the root node's key is not more extreme, swap it with the most extreme child key, then recursively heapify that child's subtree. The child subtrees must be heaps to start.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heapify

nodes.label: heap property
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines heap property as: Each node in a tree has a key which is more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the key of its parent .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heapproperty

nodes.label: height
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines height as: The maximum distance of any node from the root . If a tree has only one node (the root), the height is zero. The height of an empty tree is not defined.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: height

nodes.label: height-balanced binary search tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines height-balanced binary search tree as: A height-balanced tree which is also a binary search tree . It supports membership, insert, and delete operations in time logarithmic in the number of nodes in the tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heightBalancedBinSrchTree

nodes.label: height-balanced tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines height-balanced tree as: A tree whose subtrees differ in height by no more than one and the subtrees are height-balanced, too. An empty tree is height-balanced.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heightBalancedTree

nodes.label: heuristic
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines heuristic as: An algorithm that usually, but not always, works or that gives nearly the right answer.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heuristic

nodes.label: histogram sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines histogram sort as: An efficient 3-pass refinement of a bucket sort algorithm. The first pass counts the number of items for each bucket in an auxiliary array , and then makes a running total so each auxiliary entry is the number of preceding items. The second pass puts each item in its proper bucket according to the auxiliary entry for the key of that item. The last pass sorts each bucket. Also known as interpolation sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: histogramSort

nodes.label: homeomorphic
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines homeomorphic as: Two graphs are homeomorphic if they can be made isomorphic by inserting new vertices of degree 2 into edges .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: homeomorphic

nodes.label: horizontal visibility map
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines horizontal visibility map as: A partition of the plane into regions by drawing a horizontal straight line through each vertex p of a planar straight-line graph until it intersects an edge e of the graph or extends to infinity. The edge e is said to be horizontally visible from p.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: horizontalVisMap

nodes.label: hsadelta
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hsadelta as: An algorithm to produce a sequence of insert and copy commands (an edit script ) which creates a new version file from a reference file. To begin, hash every block of the reference file and store every hash in a hash value array . Build a suffix array and three other data structures for quick access. Beginning at the first location in the version file, hash a block and look for the longest match in the reference file. Upon a match, encode an insert back to the previous match and a copy of the match. If no match, look at the next location. At the end, encode an insert for remaining unmatched characters.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hsadelta

nodes.label: hybrid algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hybrid algorithm as: Any algorithm composed of simpler algorithms.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hybridAlgorithm

nodes.label: hyperedge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines hyperedge as: A connection between any number of vertices of a hypergraph . Formal Definition: A hyperedge is a set of vertices of a hypergraph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hyperedge

nodes.label: ideal random shuffle
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ideal random shuffle as: A permutation algorithm, or shuffle, that has exactly the same chance of producing any permutation.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: idealRandomShuffle

nodes.label: ideal merge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ideal merge as: Merge n sorted streams into one output stream. To begin the streams are sorted by the value of the head element of each. Then the head of the first stream, which is the least since the streams were sorted, is removed and written to the output. That stream is inserted back into the list of streams according to its new head. Taking the head of the first stream and reinserting that stream is repeated until all elements have been processed. Using linear search to insert a stream into the list, the execution time is Θ(M N) where M is the total number of elements. Keeping the streams in a heap , the execution time is Θ(M log N) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: idealmerge

nodes.label: implication
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines implication as: The boolean implies function.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: implication

nodes.label: implies
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines implies as: Implication: 0 → 0 = 1, 0 → 1 = 1, 1 → 0 = 0, 1 → 1 = 1.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: implies

nodes.label: incompressible string
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines incompressible string as: A string whose Kolmogorov complexity equals its length, so that it has no shorter encodings.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: incompressbl

nodes.label: in-degree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines in-degree as: The number of edges coming into a vertex in a directed graph .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: indegree

nodes.label: independent set
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines independent set as: A set of vertices in a graph such that for any pair of vertices, there is no edge between them.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: independentSet

nodes.label: index file
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines index file as: A file which stores keys and an index into another file. The index file may have additional structure, e.g., be a B-tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: indexfile

nodes.label: information theoretic bound
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines information theoretic bound as: lower bounds on the execution of a computation based on the rate at which information can be accumulated.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: information

nodes.label: in-order traversal
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines in-order traversal as: Process all nodes of a tree by recursively processing the left subtree, then processing the root , and finally the right subtree. Also known as symmetric traversal.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inorderTraversal

nodes.label: integer polyhedron
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines integer polyhedron as: A polyhedron , all of whose extreme points are integer valued.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: integer

nodes.label: integer linear program
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines integer linear program as: A linear program with additional constraints that all of the variables must take on integer values. Solving such problems is NP-hard .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: integerliner

nodes.label: integer multi-commodity flow
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines integer multi-commodity flow as: A multi-commodity flow in which the flow of each commodity through each edge must take an integer value. The term is also used to capture the multi-commodity flow problem in which each demand is routed along a single path.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: integermulti

nodes.label: interactive proof system
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines interactive proof system as: A protocol in which one or more provers try to convince another party, called the verifier, that the prover(s) possess certain true knowledge, such as the membership of a string x in a given language , often with the goal of revealing no further details about this knowledge. The prover(s) and verifier are formally defined as probabilistic Turing machines with special "interaction tapes" for exchanging messages.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: interactvprf

nodes.label: interior-based representation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines interior-based representation as: A representation of a region that is based on its interior (i.e., the cells that compose it).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: interiorbasd

nodes.label: internal node
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines internal node as: A node of a tree that has one or more child nodes, equivalently, one that is not a leaf . Also known as nonterminal node.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: internalnode

nodes.label: interpolation-sequential search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines interpolation-sequential search as: An approximate location is interpolated from the first and last items of a sorted array , then a linear search finds the actual location.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: interpsequen

nodes.label: intersection
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines intersection as: The intersection of two sets is a set having those members which are in both sets.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: intersection

nodes.label: intractable
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines intractable as: A problem for which no algorithm can exist which computes all instances of it in polynomial time .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: intractable

nodes.label: introspective sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines introspective sort as: A variant of quicksort which switches to heapsort for pathological inputs, that is, when execution time is becoming quadratic. Also known as introsort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: introspectiveSort

nodes.label: inverse suffix array
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inverse suffix array as: For each position in a string , the inverse suffix array has its index in the string's suffix array . Formal Definition: Given a suffix array, sa, and the corresponding inverse suffix array, isa, isa[i] = j iff sa[j] = i.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inverseSuffixArray

nodes.label: inversion list
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inversion list as: A set of non-overlapping numeric ranges, stored in an array in increasing order. Items in odd indexes begin ranges, and items in even indexes are the first number after the ends. Use a form of binary search to determine if a number is in any of the ranges. If the search ends on an odd index (a beginning), the number is in the set. If the search ends on an even index (a just-after-end) or outside the array, it is not in the set.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inversionList

nodes.label: inverted file index
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inverted file index as: An inverted index that only indicates the text in which a word appears, not where the word appears within the text.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: invertedFileIndex

nodes.label: inverted index
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines inverted index as: An index into a set of texts of the words in the texts. The index is accessed by some search method. Each index entry gives the word and a list of texts, possibly with locations within the text, where the word occurs.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: invertedIndex

nodes.label: invertible Bloom lookup table
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines invertible Bloom lookup table as: Algorithms and an array of cells to store key/value pairs. Each cell has a count of how many pairs are mapped to the cell, the sum of the keys mapped to it, and the sum of the values mapped to it. Using k hash functions , each pair is mapped to T[h 1 (k)], T[h 2 (k)], ..., T[h k (k)]. Also known as IBLT.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: invertibleBloomTable

nodes.label: irreflexive
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines irreflexive as: A binary relation R for which there is no element a such that a R a.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: irreflexive

nodes.label: isomorphic
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines isomorphic as: Two graphs are isomorphic if there is a one-to-one correspondence between their vertices and there is an edge between two vertices of one graph if and only if there is an edge between the two corresponding vertices in the other graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: isomorphic

nodes.label: J sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines J sort as: An in-place sort algorithm that uses strand sort to sort fewer than about 40 items and shuffle sort to sort more.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: j_sort

nodes.label: Jaro-Winkler
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Jaro-Winkler as: A measure of similarity between two strings . The Jaro measure is the weighted sum of percentage of matched characters from each file and transposed characters. Winkler increased this measure for matching initial characters, then rescaled it by a piecewise function, whose intervals and weights depend on the type of string (first name, last name, street, etc.).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: jaroWinkler

nodes.label: jelly-fish
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines jelly-fish as: A theoretical data structure for n items. It starts with a balanced binary search tree of about √(n) nodes. The leaf nodes lead to "tentacles" or linked lists , each of about √(n) nodes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: jellyfish

nodes.label: Johnson-Trotter
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Johnson-Trotter as: Generate permutations by swapping one adjacent pair of elements at a time. Also known as Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter, Trotter-Johnson.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: johnsonTrotter

nodes.label: Johnson's algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Johnson's algorithm as: An algorithm to solve the all pairs shortest path problem in a sparse weighted, directed graph . First, it adds a new node with zero weight edges from it to all other nodes, and runs the Bellman-Ford algorithm to check for negative weight cycles and find h(v), the least weight of a path from the new node to node v. Next it reweights the edges using the nodes' h(v) values. Finally for each node, it runs Dijkstra's algorithm and stores the computed least weight to other nodes, reweighted using the nodes' h(v) values, as the final weight. The time complexity is O(V²log V + VE) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: johnsonsAlgorithm

nodes.label: k²-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k²-tree as: A compact representation of a sparse directed graph . It requires 1 to 3 bits per edge. Many access functions, like successor(s), predecessor(s), and range (all links from a range of vertices to another range of vertices), have very efficient implementations.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: k2tree

nodes.label: Karnaugh map
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Karnaugh map as: A method for minimizing a boolean expression , usually aided by a rectangular map of the value of the expression for all possible input values. Input values are arranged in a Gray code . Maximal rectangular groups that cover the inputs where the expression is true give a minimum implementation. Also known as Veitch diagram, KV diagram.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karnaughmap

nodes.label: Karp-Rabin
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Karp-Rabin as: A string matching algorithm that compares string's hash values, rather than the strings themselves. For efficiency, the hash value of the next position in the text is easily computed from the hash value of the current position. Also known as Rabin-Karp.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karpRabin

nodes.label: Karp reduction
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Karp reduction as: A reduction given by a polynomial time computable transformation function.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karpreductin

nodes.label: k-ary Huffman coding
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-ary Huffman coding as: A minimal variable-length coding based on the frequency of each character. Similar to a Huffman coding , but joins k trees into a k-ary tree at each step, and uses k symbols for each level.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karyHuffman

nodes.label: k-ary tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-ary tree as: A tree with no more than k children for each node . Also known as k-way tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karyTree

nodes.label: k-ary heap
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-ary heap as: A complete tree where every node has a key more extreme (greater or less) than the key of its parent . Each node has k or fewer children .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karyheap

nodes.label: k-coloring
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-coloring as: 1) The assignment of k colors (or any distinct marks) to the vertices of a graph . 2) The assignment of k colors to the edges of a graph . A coloring is a proper coloring if no two adjacent vertices or edges have the same color.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kcoloring

nodes.label: k-connected graph
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-connected graph as: A connected graph such that deleting any k-1 vertices (and incident edges ) results in a graph that is still connected.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kconnectedGraph

nodes.label: k-d-B-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-d-B-tree as: A data structure which splits multidimensional spaces like an adaptive k-d tree , but balances the resulting tree like a B-tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kdbtree

nodes.label: k-dimensional
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-dimensional as: (1) Dealing with or restricted to a space where location can be completely described with exactly k orthogonal axes. (2) Dealing with a space of any number of dimensions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kdimensional

nodes.label: K-dominant match
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines K-dominant match as: A match [i,j] having rank k and such that for any other pair [i',j'] of rank k either i'>i and j'≤ j or i' ≤ i and j'>j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kdominant

nodes.label: k-d tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-d tree as: A multidimensional search tree for points in k dimensional space. Levels of the tree are split along successive dimensions at the points.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kdtree

nodes.label: key
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines key as: The part of a group of data by which it is sorted, indexed, cross referenced, etc.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: key

nodes.label: knight's tour
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines knight's tour as: A series of moves of a chess knight that visits all squares on the board exactly once.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: knightstour

nodes.label: Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm as: A string matching algorithm that turns the search string into a finite state machine , then runs the machine with the string to be searched as the input string. Execution time is O(m+n) , where m is the length of the search string, and n is the length of the string to be searched. Also known as KMP.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: knuthMorrisPratt

nodes.label: Kolmogorov complexity
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Kolmogorov complexity as: The minimum number of bits into which a string can be compressed without losing information. This is defined with respect to a fixed, but universal decompression scheme, given by a universal Turing machine .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kolmogorov

nodes.label: Kripke structure
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Kripke structure as: A nondeterministic finite state machine whose states are labeled with boolean variables, which are the evaluations of expressions in that state. It may be extended with fairness constraints.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kripkeStruct

nodes.label: k-way merge sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines k-way merge sort as: A merge sort that sorts a data stream using repeated merges. It distributes the input into k streams by repeatedly reading a block of input that fits in memory, called a run , sorting it, then writing it to the next stream. It merges runs from the k streams into an output stream. It then repeatedly distributes the runs in the output stream to the k streams and merges them until there is a single sorted output. Also known as p-way merge sort.

nodes.label: little-o notation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines little-o notation as: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. Also known as decimation.
