nodes.label: pseudo-random number generator
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pseudo-random number generator as: A deterministic algorithm to generate a sequence of numbers with little or no discernible pattern in the numbers, except for broad statistical properties. Also known as PRNG, deterministic random bit generator, DRBG.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pseudorandomNumberGen

nodes.label: P-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines P-tree as: (1) A spatial access method that defines hyperplanes, in addition to the orthogonal dimensions, which node boundaries may parallel. Space is split by hierarchically nested polytopes (multidimensional boxes with nonrectangular sides). The R-tree is a special case that has no additional hyperplanes. (2) A spatial access method that splits space by hierarchically nested polytopes. The R-tree is a special case in which all polytopes are boxes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ptree

nodes.label: purely functional language
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines purely functional language as: A language that does not allow any destructive operation---one which overwrites data---such as the assignment operation. Purely functional languages are free of side effects, i.e., invoking a function has no effect other than computing the value returned by the function.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: purelyfnctnl

nodes.label: pushdown automaton
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines pushdown automaton as: A restricted Turing machine where the tape acts as a pushdown store (or stack , where only the latest element can be read), with an extra one-way read-only input tape. Also known as PDA.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: pushdownautm

nodes.label: q sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines q sort as: The sort function in many libraries. It is generally a combination of quicksort, for many items, and insertion sort , for a few items.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: qsort

nodes.label: quadratic probing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines quadratic probing as: A method of open addressing for a hash table in which a collision is resolved by putting the item in the next empty place given by a probe sequence . The space between places in the sequence increases quadratically.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quadraticprb

nodes.label: quad trie
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines quad trie as: A tree in which each node is split according to some subset of the key , typically a character.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quadtrie

nodes.label: quantum computation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines quantum computation as: Computation based on quantum mechanical effects, such as superposition and entanglement, in addition to classical digital manipulations.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quantumComputation

nodes.label: quick search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines quick search as: A string matching algorithm that compares characters from the end of the search string to its beginning. When a character doesn't match, the next character in the text beyond the search string determines where the next possible match begins.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quicksearch

nodes.label: ragged matrix
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ragged matrix as: A matrix having irregular numbers of items in each row.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: raggedmatrix

nodes.label: random search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines random search as: Repeatedly check items in an array at random until successful.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomSearch

nodes.label: random access machine
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines random access machine as: A model of computation whose memory consists of an unbounded sequence of registers, each of which may hold an integer. In this model, arithmetic operations are allowed to compute the address of a memory register.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomaccess

nodes.label: randomized rounding
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines randomized rounding as: A probabilistic method to convert a solution of a relaxed problem into an approximate solution to the original problem.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomizdrnd

nodes.label: randomized algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines randomized algorithm as: An algorithm that makes random (or pseudorandom) choices.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomizedAlgo

nodes.label: randomized binary search tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines randomized binary search tree as: A binary search tree in which nodes have a randomly assigned priority. Updates keep priorities in heap order instead of keeping balance information and doing rebalance operations. Also known as cartesian tree, RBST.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomizedBinarySearchTree

nodes.label: randomized complexity
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines randomized complexity as: The expected running time of the best possible randomized algorithm over the worst input.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomizedComplexity

nodes.label: random sampling
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines random sampling as: Using a randomly selected sample of the data to help solve a problem on the whole data.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: randomsampl

nodes.label: range
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines range as: The possible results of a function or relation . For instance, the range of cosine is [-1,+1].

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: range

nodes.label: range sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines range sort as: A bucket sort where the function to determine the bucket is based on the range of possible keys .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rangesort

nodes.label: rank
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rank as: For a given match, this is the number of matches in a longest chain terminating with that match, inclusive.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rank

nodes.label: rapid sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rapid sort as: A 2-pass sort algorithm that is efficient when the range of keys is approximately equal to the number of items and only keys are sorted. The first pass counts the occurrences of each key in an auxiliary array . The second pass goes over the auxiliary array writing the counted number of keys to the destination.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rapidSort

nodes.label: Ratcliff/Obershelp pattern recognition
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Ratcliff/Obershelp pattern recognition as: Compute the similarity of two strings as the number of matching characters divided by the total number of characters in the two strings. Matching characters are those in the longest common substring plus, recursively, matching characters in the unmatched region on either side of the longest common substring.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ratcliffObershelp

nodes.label: reachable
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines reachable as: A vertex v is reachable from another vertex u if there is a path of any length from u to v. Also known as reachability.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reachable

nodes.label: rebalance
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rebalance as: Restore balance to a tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rebalance

nodes.label: recognizer
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recognizer as: A finite state machine with one or more states designated as accepting states . An input string is accepted if there is a path from the start state to an accepting state.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recognizer

nodes.label: rectangular matrix
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rectangular matrix as: An n × m matrix , or, one whose size may not be the same in both dimensions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rectangmatrx

nodes.label: rectilinear
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rectilinear as: Distance, paths, lines, etc. which are always parallel to axes at right angles. For example, a path along the streets of Salt Lake City or the moves of a rook in chess.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rectilinear

nodes.label: rectilinear Steiner tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rectilinear Steiner tree as: A minimum-length rectilinear tree connecting a set of points, called terminals , in the plane. This tree may include points other than the terminals, which are called Steiner points .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rectilinearSteinertree

nodes.label: recurrence relation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recurrence relation as: The specification of a sequence of values in terms of earlier values in the sequence and base values. Also known as recurrence equations.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recurrence

nodes.label: recursion tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursion tree as: A method to analyze the complexity of an algorithm by diagramming the recursive function calls. Formal Definition: A recursion tree T(p) of degree p is either (i) null or (ii) has p children which are recursion trees.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursionTree

nodes.label: recursion termination
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursion termination as: The point when conditions are met and a recursive algorithm ceases calling itself and begins to return values.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursiontrm

nodes.label: recursive
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursive as: (1) A data structure that is partially composed of other instances of the data structure. For instance, a tree is composed of smaller trees ( subtrees ) and leaf nodes , and a list may have other lists as elements. (2) An algorithm in which functions might call themselves. For instance, quicksort or heapify .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursive

nodes.label: recursively enumerable language
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursively enumerable language as: A language accepted by a Turing machine .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursivelyEnumerableLang

nodes.label: recursive data structure
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines recursive data structure as: A data structure that is partially composed of smaller or simpler instances of the same data structure. For instance, a tree is composed of smaller trees ( subtrees ) and leaf nodes , and a list may have other lists as elements.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursivstrc

nodes.label: reduced basis
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines reduced basis as: A basis for a lattice that is nearly orthogonal.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reducedbasis

nodes.label: reduction
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines reduction as: A computable transformation of one problem into another.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reduction

nodes.label: reflexive
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines reflexive as: A binary relation R for which a R a for all a.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reflexive

nodes.label: regular decomposition
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines regular decomposition as: A space decomposition method that partitions the underlying space by recursively halving it across the various dimensions instead of permitting the partitioning lines to vary.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: regular

nodes.label: relation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines relation as: A computation which takes some inputs and yields an output. Any particular input may yield different outputs at different times. Formally, a mapping from each element in the domain to one or more elements in the range .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: relation

nodes.label: relational structure
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines relational structure as: The counterpart in formal logic of a data structure or class instance in the object-oriented sense. Examples are strings , directed graphs , and undirected graphs . Sets of relational structures generalize the notion of languages as sets of strings.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: relational

nodes.label: relative performance guarantee
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines relative performance guarantee as: The maximum ratio by which the result of a ρ-approximation algorithm may depart from the optimal solution . Also known as performance ratio.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: relativePerformGuar

nodes.label: relaxation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines relaxation as: An optimization problem with an enlarged feasible region (and extended objective function ) compared with an original optimization problem. Typically, the relaxation is considerably easier to solve than the original.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: relaxation

nodes.label: relaxed balance
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines relaxed balance as: When rebalancing a search tree is independent of updating the tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: relaxedBalance

nodes.label: repeated squaring
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines repeated squaring as: Compute the n th power of an expression in Θ(log n) steps by repeatedly squaring an intermediate result and multiplying an accumulating value by the intermediate result when appropriate.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: repeatedSquaring

nodes.label: rescalable
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rescalable as: An optimization for which given any instance of the problem and integer λ >0, there is an easily computed second instance that is the same except that the objective function for the second instance is (element-wise) λ times the objective function of the first instance. For such problems, the best one can hope for is a relative performance guarantee , not an absolute performance guarantee .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rescalable

nodes.label: reservoir sampling
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines reservoir sampling as: Randomly select k items from a stream of items of unknown length. Save the first k items in an array of size k. For each item j, j > k, choose a random integer M from 1 to j (inclusive). If M ≤ k, replace item M of the array with item j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reservoirSampling

nodes.label: restricted universe sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines restricted universe sort as: A sort algorithm that operates on the basis that the keys are members of a restricted set of values. They may not require comparisons of keys to perform the sorting.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: restricted

nodes.label: R-file
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines R-file as: A spatial access method which divides space into a hierarchically of nested boxes. Objects are indexed in the lowest cell which completely contains them.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rfile

nodes.label: ρ-approximation algorithm
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ρ-approximation algorithm as: An approximation algorithm guaranteed to find a solution at most (or at least, as appropriate) ρ times the optimum. The ratio ρ is the performance ratio or relative performance guarantee of the algorithm.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rhoapproxmtn

nodes.label: Rice's method
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Rice's method as: A method of complex asymptotics that can handle certain alternating sums arising in the analysis of algorithms.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ricesmethod

nodes.label: right-threaded tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines right-threaded tree as: A variant of a threaded tree in which only the right thread, i.e. link to the successor, of each node is maintained.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rightThreadedTree

nodes.label: right rotation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines right rotation as: (1) In a binary search tree , pushing a node N down and to the right to balance the tree. N's left child replaces N, and the left child's right child becomes N's left child. (2) In an array , moving all items to the next higher location. The last item is moved to the first location, which is now vacant. (3) In a list , removing the tail and inserting it at the head . Also known as rotate right.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rightrotatn

nodes.label: Robin Hood hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Robin Hood hashing as: In case of collision , the item with the longer probe sequence stays in the position. The other item is moved. This tends to equalize the length of probe sequences.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: robinHoodHashing

nodes.label: rooted tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rooted tree as: A tree in which one node is designated as the root . Also known as oriented tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rootedtree

nodes.label: rotation
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines rotation as: To switch children and parents among two or three adjacent nodes to restore balance to a tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rotation

nodes.label: RP
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines RP as: The class of languages for which membership can be determined in polynomial time by a probabilistic Turing machine with no false acceptances and less than half false rejections. "RP" means " R andomized P olynomial" time. Formal Definition: For a language, S, there exists a probabilistic Turing machine , M, that accepts or rejects any string in polynomial time . If w ∉ S, M rejects w. If w ∈ S, M accepts w with a probability at least 1/2. Also known as randomized polynomial time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rp

nodes.label: R-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines R-tree as: (1) A spatial access method that splits space with hierarchically nested, and possibly overlapping, boxes. The tree is height-balanced. (2) A recursion tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rtree

nodes.label: run time
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines run time as: (1) The amount of time needed to execute an algorithm . (2) The time when a compiled program is executing, versus compile time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: runtime

nodes.label: saturated edge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines saturated edge as: An edge in a flow network which has the maximum possible flow.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: saturatedEdge

nodes.label: SBB tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines SBB tree as: A symmetric binary B-tree. Now known as a red-black tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sbbtree

nodes.label: scan
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines scan as: A parallel operation in which each element in an array or linked list receives the sum of all previous elements. Also known as prefix sums.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: scan

nodes.label: scapegoat tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines scapegoat tree as: A binary search tree that needs no balance information. Search time is logarithmic , and the amortized cost of update is logarithmic .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: scapegoatTree

nodes.label: search tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines search tree as: A tree where every subtree of a node has keys less than any other subtree of the node to its right. The keys in a node are conceptually between subtrees and are greater than any keys in subtrees to its left and less than any keys in subtrees to its right.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: searchtree

nodes.label: search tree property
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines search tree property as: When the key of every node of a binary tree is larger than the key of its left child and smaller than its right child.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: searchtrprop

nodes.label: secant search
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines secant search as: Search a sorted array by estimating the next position to check based on the values at the two previous positions checked.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: secantSearch

nodes.label: secondary clustering
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines secondary clustering as: The tendency for some collision resolution schemes to create long run of filled slots away from a key hash position, e.g., along the probe sequence .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: secondaryClustering

nodes.label: segment
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines segment as: (1) The substring of a pattern delimited by two don't cares or one don't care and beginning or end of the pattern. (2) A substring .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: segment

nodes.label: Select
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Select as: A four-part algorithm to select the k th smallest element of an array . Part 1) Consider the array as groups of 5 elements; sort and find the median of each group. 2) Use Select recursively to find x , the median of the medians. 3) Next partition the array around x . 4) Let i be the number of elements in the low side of the partition. If k ≤ i, use Select recursively to find the k th element of the low side. Otherwise Select the k-i th element of the high side.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: select

nodes.label: select and partition
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines select and partition as: Given an array A of n elements and a positive integer k ≤ n, find the k th smallest element of A and partition the array such that A[1], …, A[k-1] ≤ A[k] ≤ A[k+1], …, A[n].

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectAndPartition

nodes.label: select mode
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines select mode as: An algorithm to find the mode, or most frequently occurring value, in a group of elements.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectmode

nodes.label: self-organizing list
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines self-organizing list as: A list that reorders the elements based on some self-organizing heuristic [Wikipedia] to improve average access time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selfOrganizingList

nodes.label: self-loop
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines self-loop as: An edge of a graph which starts and ends at the same vertex .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selfloop

nodes.label: semidefinite programming
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines semidefinite programming as: A generalization of a linear program in which any subset of the variables may be constrained to form a semidefinite matrix.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: semidefinite

nodes.label: separate chaining
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines separate chaining as: A scheme in which each position in the hash table has a list to handle collisions . Each position may be just a link to the list ( direct chaining ) or may be an item and a link, essentially, the head of a list. In the latter, one item is in the table, and other colliding items are in the list. Also known as external chaining.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: separateChaining

nodes.label: separation theorem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines separation theorem as: A theorem showing that two complexity classes are distinct. Most separation theorems have been proved by diagonalization .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: separatnthrm

nodes.label: set packing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines set packing as: An optimization problem to find the largest number of mutually disjoint subsets that cover a given set of sets .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: setpacking

nodes.label: shadow heap
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shadow heap as: A heap , implemented in an array , adjacent to an unordered table. The shadow is the table nodes and all their (recursive) parents , by array index, in the heap.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shadowheap

nodes.label: shadow merge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shadow merge as: An algorithm to merge two heaps by concatenating the smaller heap to the larger, then reordering just the concatenated nodes and their parents to restore the heap property.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shadowmerge

nodes.label: shadow merge insert
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shadow merge insert as: An algorithm to insert a new node into a shadow heap . The new node is placed in the unordered table. When the table grows beyond some threshold size, table nodes and all their parents are reordered so everything is a heap.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shadowmrgins

nodes.label: Shannon-Fano coding
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Shannon-Fano coding as: A variable-length coding based on the frequency of occurrence of each character. Divide the characters into two sets with the frequency of each set as close to half as possible, and assign the sets either 0 or 1 coding. Repeatedly divide the sets until each character has a unique coding.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shannonFano

nodes.label: shared memory
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shared memory as: All processors have the same global image of (and access to) all of the memory.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sharedmemory

nodes.label: Shift-Or
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines Shift-Or as: A string matching algorithm which keeps an array of bits, R, showing if prefixes of the pattern don't match at the current place. Before searching, mismatch arrays are computed for each character in the alphabet and saved in an array, S. For the next position, with the character c, R = shift(R) or S[c]. If the last bit of R is 0, the pattern matches.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shiftOr

nodes.label: shortest common supersequence
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shortest common supersequence as: Find the shortest string that contains two or more strings as subsequences .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shortestCommonSuperseq

nodes.label: shortest common superstring
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shortest common superstring as: Find the shortest string that contains two or more strings as substrings .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shortestCommonSuperstring

nodes.label: shuffle sort
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines shuffle sort as: A distribution sort algorithm that begins by removing the first 1/8 of the n items, sorting them (recursively), and putting them in an array. This creates n/8 buckets to which the remaining 7/8 of the items are distributed. Each bucket is then sorted, and the buckets are concatenated.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shuffleSort

nodes.label: sibling
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sibling as: A node in a tree that has the same parent as another node is its sibling.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sibling

nodes.label: sieve of Eratosthenes
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sieve of Eratosthenes as: An algorithm to find all prime numbers up to a certain N. Begin with an (unmarked) array of integers from 2 to N. The first unmarked integer, 2, is the first prime. Mark every multiple of this prime. Repeatedly take the next unmarked integer as the next prime and mark every multiple of the prime.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sieve

nodes.label: sift up
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sift up as: Restoring the heap property by swapping a node with its parent , and repeating the process on the parent until the root is reached or the heap property is satisfied.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: siftup

nodes.label: signature
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines signature as: The types or domains , and order, in some representations, of inputs to and outputs from a function .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: signature

nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines ∼ as: (1) Proportional to. (2) Asymptotically equal to. A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. Informally, saying some equation f(n) ∼ g(n) means it grows at the same rate as g(n). More formally, it means lim x → ∞ f(x)/g(x) = 1.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sim

nodes.label: simple uniform hashing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simple uniform hashing as: The assumption or goal that items are equally likely to hash to any value.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simpleUniformHashing

nodes.label: simple merge
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simple merge as: Merge n sorted streams into one output stream. All the stream heads are compared, and the head with the least key is removed and written to the output. This is repeated until all streams are empty.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplemerge

nodes.label: simple path
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simple path as: A path that repeats no vertex , except that the first and last may be the same vertex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplepath

nodes.label: simplex
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simplex as: The simplest N-dimensional polytope . The generalization of a triangle (2D) or tetrahedron (3D).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplex

nodes.label: simulated annealing
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simulated annealing as: A technique to find a good solution to an optimization problem by trying random variations of the current solution. A worse variation is accepted as the new solution with a probability that decreases as the computation proceeds. The slower the cooling schedule , or rate of decrease, the more likely the algorithm is to find an optimal or near- optimal solution .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simulatedAnnealing

nodes.label: simulation theorem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines simulation theorem as: One kind of computation can be simulated by another kind within stated complexity bounds. Most known containment or equality relationships between complexity classes were proved this way.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simulatnthrm

nodes.label: single-destination shortest-path problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines single-destination shortest-path problem as: Find the shortest path from each vertex in a weighted, directed graph to a specific destination vertex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singleDestShortestPath

nodes.label: single-source shortest-path problem
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines single-source shortest-path problem as: Find the shortest paths from a specific source vertex to every other vertex in a weighted, directed graph . Dijkstra's algorithm solves this if all weights are nonnegative. The Bellman-Ford algorithm handles any weights.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singleSourceShortestPath

nodes.label: single program multiple data
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines single program multiple data as: The dominant style of parallel programming, where all processors use the same program, though each has its own data. Also known as SPMD.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singleprogrm

nodes.label: singularity analysis
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines singularity analysis as: A complex asymptotic technique for determining the asymptotics of certain algebraic functions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singularity

nodes.label: sink
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines sink as: A vertex of a directed graph with no outgoing edges . More formally, a vertex with with out-degree 0.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sink

nodes.label: skd-tree
nodes.summary: NIST DADS defines skd-tree as: The spatial k-d tree is a spatial access method where successive levels are split along different dimensions. Objects are indexed by their centroid , and the minimum bounding box of objects in a node are stored in the node.

nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Surgery, Plastic as: The branch of surgery concerned with restoration, reconstruction, or improvement of defective, damaged, or missing structures.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D013518

nodes.label: Surgical Oncology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Surgical Oncology as: A surgical specialty concerned with management of cancer.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000071077

nodes.label: Thoracic Surgery
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Thoracic Surgery as: A surgical specialty concerned with diagnosis and treatment of disorders of the heart, lungs, and esophagus. Two major types of thoracic surgery are classified as pulmonary and cardiovascular.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D013903

nodes.label: Sports Nutritional Sciences
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Sports Nutritional Sciences as: The study of NUTRITION PROCESSES during EXERCISE and ATHLETIC PERFORMANCE as well as specific NUTRITIONAL REQUIREMENTS of ATHLETES and the relationship between NUTRITIONAL STATUS and NUTRITION DISORDERS in athletes.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D064132

nodes.label: Veterinary Sports Medicine
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Veterinary Sports Medicine as: The field of veterinary medicine concerned with PHYSICAL FITNESS of animals in sports (horse racing, dog racing, etc.) and the diagnosis and treatment of sports injuries in animals.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D064796

nodes.label: Evidence-Based Emergency Medicine
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Evidence-Based Emergency Medicine as: A way of providing emergency medical care that is guided by a thoughtful integration of the best available scientific knowledge with clinical expertise in EMERGENCY MEDICINE . This approach allows the practitioner to critically assess research data, clinical guidelines, and other information resources in order to correctly identify the clinical problem, apply the most high-quality intervention, and re-evaluate the outcome for future improvement.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D055416

nodes.label: Cardiac Electrophysiology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Cardiac Electrophysiology as: The study of the electrical activity and characteristics of the HEART ; MYOCARDIUM ; and CARDIOMYOCYTES .

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D054849

nodes.label: Cardio-Oncology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Cardio-Oncology as: The study, diagnosis, and treatment of CARDIOTOXICITY in patients who undergo treatment for cancer.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000097562

nodes.label: Transfusion Medicine
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Transfusion Medicine as: The area of hematology that is concerned with the transfusion of blood and blood components, and in prevention and treatment of adverse effects from BLOOD TRANSFUSION errors.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D064826

nodes.label: Psycho-Oncology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Psycho-Oncology as: A specialty which deals with the interrelationship of physical, psychological, social, behavioral, and ethical aspects of cancer. Psycho-oncology examines the behavioral and psychosocial factors that may influence the course of the disease, cancer risk, prevention, and detection.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000073320

nodes.label: Preventive Psychiatry
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Preventive Psychiatry as: A discipline concerned with the prevention of mental illness and the promotion of mental health.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D011316

nodes.label: Molecular Epidemiology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Molecular Epidemiology as: The application of molecular biology to the answering of epidemiological questions. The examination of patterns of changes in DNA to implicate particular carcinogens and the use of molecular markers to predict which individuals are at highest risk for a disease are common examples.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D017720

nodes.label: Pharmacoepidemiology
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Pharmacoepidemiology as: The science concerned with the benefit and risk of drugs used in populations and the analysis of the outcomes of drug therapies. Pharmacoepidemiologic data come from both clinical trials and epidemiological studies with emphasis on methods for the detection and evaluation of drug-related adverse effects, assessment of risk vs benefit ratios in drug therapy, patterns of drug utilization, the cost-effectiveness of specific drugs, methodology of postmarketing surveillance, and the relation between pharmacoepidemiology and the formulation and interpretation of regulatory guidelines. (Pharmacoepidemiol Drug Saf 1992;1(1); J Pharmacoepidemiol 1990;1(1))

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D017891

nodes.label: Earth sciences
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Earth sciences as: Broad term for all science related to the study of the earth. This category is also used for geosciences

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 291

nodes.label: Geologic time periods
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Geologic time periods as: This category is also used for geologic age and geologic time

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1634

nodes.label: Hazards
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Hazards as: Potential dangers from both natural processes (e.g., earthquakes, floods, and climate change) and human impacts on the environment. This category is also used for catastrophes , with coastal processes for coastal hazards , disasters , with earthquakes for earthquake hazards , emergency management resources , environmental hazards , geologic hazards , with algal blooms for harmful algal blooms , and with ocean processes for ocean hazards

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 531

nodes.label: Earth characteristics
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Earth characteristics as: The measurable, definable properties and features of the earth.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 287

nodes.label: Atmospheric sciences
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Atmospheric sciences as: Studies relating to composition, structure, physics, chemistry, and dynamics of the atmosphere.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 68

nodes.label: Geography
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Geography as: Study of the earth's landforms, topography, and climate, the distribution of flora and fauna, and the distribution, culture, and activities of human populations. This category is also used for geographic information sciences

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 447

nodes.label: Geophysics
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Geophysics as: Branch of geology studying the physical characteristics and phenomena of the earth and its atmosphere. This category is also used with maps and atlases for geophysical maps

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 470

nodes.label: Ocean sciences
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Ocean sciences as: Sciences involved in the study of geological, biological, chemical, and physical characteristics and processes of the oceans. This category is also used for oceanography and physical oceanography

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 818

nodes.label: Soil sciences
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Soil sciences as: Earth sciences dealing with the origin, classification, physical, chemical, and biological properties of soils. This category is also used for pedology (soils)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1081

nodes.label: Phanerozoic
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Phanerozoic as: Eon of geologic time approximately 542 million years ago extending to the present. https://doi.org/10.3133/fs20103059

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1652

nodes.label: Precambrian
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Precambrian as: General interval of geologic time before approximately 542 million years ago. https://doi.org/10.3133/fs20103059 This category is also used for cryptozoic

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1655

nodes.label: Atmospheric properties
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Atmospheric properties as: Characteristics of the mass of gases surrounding the earth such as composition, temperature, pressure, and humidity. This category is also used for atmosphere properties

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 67

nodes.label: Earth material properties
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Earth material properties as: Physical characteristics of rocks and unconsolidated earth materials such as soils and sediments.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1367

nodes.label: Earth structure
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Earth structure as: Major interior structural features of the planet earth.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 292

nodes.label: Geologic history
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Geologic history as: Record (and inferred reconstruction) of the origin and development of the earth since its formation. This category is also used for chronostratigraphy and geohistory

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 455

nodes.label: Geologic structure
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Geologic structure as: General position of rocks in an area, and geometrical relationships among rocks.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 459

nodes.label: Gravitational field (earth)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Gravitational field (earth) as: Region or space around earth's mass which exerts a force that mutually attracts other masses in proportion to the product of the two masses and the distance between them. This category is also used for gravity , with maps and atlases for gravity anomaly maps , and gravity field

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 501

nodes.label: Lakebed characteristics
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Lakebed characteristics as: Characteristics of the bottom of inland bodies of water. This category is also used for lake-bed characteristics , lake-bottom characteristics , and lake-floor characteristics

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2090

nodes.label: Land surface characteristics
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Land surface characteristics as: Features and attributes of earth's land surface. This category is also used for landscape and physiography

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 626

nodes.label: Magnetic field (earth)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Magnetic field (earth) as: The magnetic region surrounding earth. It is generated by the dipolar characteristic of earth's core whereby earth itself acts as a great spherical magnet with poles near, but not exactly at, the North and South poles. This category is also used for geomagnetic field , geomagnetics , geomagnetism , with maps and atlases for magnetic anomaly maps , magnetic field , and magnetosphere

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 677

nodes.label: Ocean characteristics
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Ocean characteristics as: The attributes and process of seas and oceans. This category is also used for ocean mixed-layer depth , with field inventory and monitoring for ocean monitoring , ocean surface characteristics , with ocean processes for oceans , and sea surface reflectance

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 810

nodes.label: Rocks and deposits
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Rocks and deposits as: Solid masses that make up the earth's crust as well as accumulations of materials. Use for major rock types and unconsolidated deposits. For deposits of economic value, see related terms. This category is also used for crystals , with maps and atlases for lithologic maps , lithology , and rock composition

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1005

nodes.label: Snow and ice cover
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Snow and ice cover as: Accumulation of snow or ice blanketing land surfaces. This category is also used for cryosphere , glaciers , ice , with drilling and coring for ice core sampling , and snowpack

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1072

nodes.label: Stratigraphic sections
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Stratigraphic sections as: Vertical arrangement in layers of rock units whose sequence is used to study the geological history of the strata. This category is also used for geologic sections , geologic units , sections (geologic) , sections (stratigraphic) , strata , and stratum

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1103

nodes.label: Topography
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Topography as: Configuration of the land surface and sea floor. This category is also used for elevation and relief

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1176

nodes.label: Soil chemistry
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Soil chemistry as: Branch of chemistry concerned with the elements and compounds that make up soils. Includes chemical processes involving soils.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1078

nodes.label: Water chemistry
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Water chemistry as: Branch of chemistry that deals with the elements and compounds in water.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1298

nodes.label: Paleogeography
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Paleogeography as: Study of the history of earth surface characteristics; geomorphology in the past.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1679

nodes.label: Economic geology
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Economic geology as: Scientific study of the formation, location, and use of marketable geologic materials including fuels, metals, minerals, and water.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 312

nodes.label: Marine geology
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Marine geology as: Branch of geology concerned with the composition, geologic history, and earth processes of the ocean floor and the continental margin. This category is also used for geological oceanography

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 706

nodes.label: Structural geology
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Structural geology as: Branch of geology concerned with the distribution, position, shape, and internal structure of rocks.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1117

nodes.label: Geodesy
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Geodesy as: Branch of science dealing with measuring the earth or large areas of the earth for making maps, determining the size and shape of the earth, and correlating gravitational, geological, and magnetic surveys of the earth.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 440

nodes.label: Marine geophysics
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Marine geophysics as: Branch of earth sciences concerned with the physical processes of the oceans and continental margins. We include here studies of large bodies of brackish and fresh water, such as lakes and rivers.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 707

nodes.label: Hydrodynamics
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Hydrodynamics as: Principles of fluid dynamics applied to water bodies. This category is also used for fluid dynamics

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1678

nodes.label: Paleoceanography
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Paleoceanography as: Study of the oceans in the geologic past, including their physical, chemical, biologic, and geologic history.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 859

nodes.label: Invertebrate paleontology
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Invertebrate paleontology as: Branch of paleontology which deals with fossil animals without backbones.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 604

nodes.label: Micropaleontology
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Micropaleontology as: Branch of paleontology dealing with fossils too small to be seen without a microscope.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 738

nodes.label: Paleobotany
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Paleobotany as: Branch of paleontology concerned with the study of fossil plants and plant life in the geologic past.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 858

nodes.label: Vertebrate paleontology
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Vertebrate paleontology as: Branch of paleontology dealing with fossil animals that have spinal columns.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1267

nodes.label: Cenozoic
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Cenozoic as: Era of geologic time approximately 65 million years ago extending to the present. https://doi.org/10.3133/fs20103059

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1627

nodes.label: Mesozoic
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Mesozoic as: Era of geologic time approximately 251 to 65 million years ago. https://doi.org/10.3133/fs20103059

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1640

nodes.label: Paleozoic
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Paleozoic as: Era of geologic time approximately 542 to 251 million years ago. https://doi.org/10.3133/fs20103059

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1649

nodes.label: Archaean
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Archaean as: Eon of geologic time approximately 4 to 2.5 billion years ago. https://doi.org/10.3133/fs20103059

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1622

nodes.label: Hadean
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Hadean as: Eon of geologic time prior to 4 billion years ago. https://doi.org/10.3133/fs20103059

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1635

nodes.label: Proterozoic
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Proterozoic as: Eon of geologic time approximately 2.5 billion to 542 million years ago. https://doi.org/10.3133/fs20103059

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1656

nodes.label: Air temperature
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Air temperature as: This category is also used for temperature (air)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 27

nodes.label: Atmospheric composition
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Atmospheric composition as: Components of the mass of gases that surrounds a planet. The earth's atmosphere consists of nitrogen, oxygen, and small portions of other gases. This category is also used with contamination and pollution for air pollution

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 65

nodes.label: Acid neutralizing potential
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Acid neutralizing potential as: Geochemical capacity of earth materials to affect the pH of waters flowing through them. This category is also used for acid neutralizing capacity and neutralization potential

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2276

nodes.label: Bulk density
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Bulk density as: Overall density of an unconsolidated earth material.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1714

nodes.label: Electromagnetic reflectance and emissivity
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Electromagnetic reflectance and emissivity as: Effectiveness of an earth material in reflecting or emitting radiation, varying by wavelength. Measurements are made over the infrared part of the electromagnetic spectrum in a laboratory to compare with remotely-sensed data obtained by airborne or satellite imaging systems. This category is also used for infrared reflectance , laboratory reflectance , laboratory spectra , spectral radiance , and spectral reflectance

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2290

nodes.label: Magnetism
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Magnetism as: Strength and orientation of the permanent magnetic field in a given sample of an earth material

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1741

nodes.label: Permeability
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Permeability as: The ability of fluids to pass through an earth material, typically depending on the connectedness of pore space in the material. This category is also used for soil permeability

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1368

nodes.label: Porosity
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Porosity as: The proportion of open space in a rock or unconsolidated material. This category is also used for interstices and soil porosity

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1369

nodes.label: Radioactivity
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Radioactivity as: Release of subatomic particles from earth materials. Generally the energy of these particles is used to determine the chemical elements present. This category is also used for gamma ray emission

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1701

nodes.label: Resistivity
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Resistivity as: Electrical resistance of materials, often measured in boreholes.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1712

nodes.label: Soil moisture
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Soil moisture as: Water content of soil and other near-surface unconsolidated earth material

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2027

nodes.label: Soil temperature
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Soil temperature as: Temperature and temperature gradients in soil and other near-surface unconsolidated earth materials

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2028

nodes.label: Core (earth)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Core (earth) as: The superdense center of the earth composed of two layers: a liquid outer layer and a solid inner core of metallic iron-nickel alloy.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 211

nodes.label: Crust (earth)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Crust (earth) as: The outermost layer of the earth which is relatively thin, of lower density than the core, and rocky.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 219

nodes.label: Mantle (earth)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Mantle (earth) as: Zone of earth's interior between the crust and the core. It is 2,900 kilometers (1,740 miles) thick and consists of a dense upper layer (upper mantle) and a partially molten lower layer (lower mantle), separated by a transition zone.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 690

nodes.label: Earth history
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Earth history as: The structural and compositional changes that the earth has undergone from its formation. Use for discussions of the whole earth (or large sections of it) instead of regional studies.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 288

nodes.label: Foliation (geologic)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Foliation (geologic) as: The property of rocks or glaciers splitting into thin layers or plates due to the orientation of crystals and dynamic movement.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 404

nodes.label: Lineation (geologic)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Lineation (geologic) as: Linear topographic feature on the earth's surface or in rocks. This category is also used for lineaments

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 660

nodes.label: Structure contours
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Structure contours as: Gridding and contouring lines drawn on geologic maps to depict boundaries of structural features. This category is also used with maps and atlases for depth-to maps

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1118

nodes.label: Bouguer anomaly
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Bouguer anomaly as: Gravity anomaly corrected to remove the effects of topography using knowledge of the terrain in the area surrounding the measurement station.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1675

nodes.label: Free-air anomaly
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Free-air anomaly as: Gravity anomaly corrected for elevation of the location at which the measurements were made.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1674

nodes.label: Gravity gradient
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Gravity gradient as: Lateral variation of the three-dimensional vector components of gravity, typically measured using airborne sensors. This category is also used for gravity gradiometry

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2291

nodes.label: Isostatic anomaly
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Isostatic anomaly as: Gravity anomaly corrected for the effects of low-density rocks underlying mountains.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1673

nodes.label: Lakebed acoustic reflectivity
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Lakebed acoustic reflectivity as: Acoustic energy received by a sonar system, providing a measure of the roughness of the lakebed. This category is also used for backscatter (lakebed)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2091

nodes.label: Karst
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Karst as: Landscape characterized by dissolution features in carbonate or evaporite terranes, often containing caves and sinkholes. This category is also used for karst topography and karstic

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2031

nodes.label: Ocean salinity
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Ocean salinity as: Measure of the percentage of dissolved salts in seawater.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 817

nodes.label: Ocean temperature
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Ocean temperature as: Distribution of heat in the oceans, including surface water, thermocline and mode waters, and deep waters. Includes discussion and measures of both in-situ and potential temperature. This category is also used for temperature (ocean)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 819

nodes.label: Sea-floor characteristics
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Sea-floor characteristics as: Geomorphic features and geographic, compositional, and textural variation in the materials composing the ocean floor. Includes both large-scale structures (such as seamounts and rises) and fine-scale variations in rocks and deposits on the sea floor. This category is also used for ocean bottom characteristics , sea floor characteristics , and seafloor characteristics

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1025

nodes.label: Sea-level change
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Sea-level change as: Variation in the relative vertical position of land and ocean waters. Caused globally by changes in the distribution of ice masses and the shape of the oceans, and locally by the rate of uplift or subsidence of the land surface. Includes both global (eustatic) and local (relative) sea-level variations. This category is also used for sea level change , sea level rise , and sea-level rise

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1028

nodes.label: Fossils
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Fossils as: Recognizable remains such as bones, shells, leaves, burrows, impressions, or tracks of past life on the earth. This category is also used for index fossils and microfossils

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 414

nodes.label: Igneous rocks
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Igneous rocks as: Rocks formed from melted rock that has cooled and solidified.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 572

nodes.label: Metamorphic rocks
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Metamorphic rocks as: Sedimentary or igneous rocks which have undergone such intense changes in temperature, pressure, structural stress, or chemical environment that they are transformed into denser rocks.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 725

nodes.label: Mineral deposits
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Mineral deposits as: Deposits in which particular minerals are concentrated, typically noticed and studied if the minerals have economic value. This category is also used for ore deposits

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2043

nodes.label: Permafrost
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Permafrost as: Rocks and deposits in which the interstitial waters remain perennially frozen.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1370

nodes.label: Petroleum
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Petroleum as: Naturally occurring hydrocarbons, typically fluid or gas, often of economic use. Includes oil, natural gas, and asphaltic compounds found in tar sands and oil shales. This category is also used with industrial pollution for oil spills

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1804

nodes.label: Sedimentary rocks
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Sedimentary rocks as: Rocks formed by the consolidation of loose, uncemented pieces of sediments.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1035

nodes.label: Unconsolidated deposits
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Unconsolidated deposits as: Loosely bound sediments such as sand, gravel, and silt which tend to accumulate in low areas or valleys. This category is also used for alluvium , eolian sediments , loess , with chemical analysis for sediment geochemistry , sediments , and surficial deposits

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1199

nodes.label: Sea ice concentration
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Sea ice concentration as: Proportion of ocean area in a given region that contains or is covered by floating ice. This category is also used for sea ice cover and sea-ice concentration

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1722

nodes.label: Bedrock geologic units
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Bedrock geologic units as: Units of consolidated (solid) rock that underlie soils or other unconsolidated materials. This category is also used with maps and atlases for basement maps and geologic formations

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 84

nodes.label: Geologic contacts
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Geologic contacts as: Junctions of two different rock formations varying by type or age of rock, including faults, unconformities, and bedding planes. This category is also used for contacts (geologic)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 452

nodes.label: Stratigraphic thickness
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Stratigraphic thickness as: Thickness of earth material layers or groups of such layers, often portrayed as isopachs (contours) or gridded data. This category is also used for isopach , with maps and atlases for isopach maps , sediment thickness , and with maps and atlases for stratigraphic thickness maps

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2089

nodes.label: Surficial geologic units
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Surficial geologic units as: Rock units on the earth's surface. This category is also used with maps and atlases for surficial geologic maps

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1127

nodes.label: Bathymetry
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Bathymetry as: The elevation of the earth's surface beneath a body of water, especially the ocean, typically determined by measurements of depth from the water surface. This category is also used for bathymetry data , sea floor topography , and underwater contours

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 80

nodes.label: Marine chemistry
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Marine chemistry as: Branch of chemistry that deals with the properties, composition, structure, and interaction of substances in the seas and oceans. This category is also used for chemical oceanography , ocean chemistry , and water properties (marine)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 703

nodes.label: Biostratigraphy
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Biostratigraphy as: Branch of geology concerned with the separation and differentiation of rock units based on the fossils they contain.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 115

nodes.label: Lithostratigraphy
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Lithostratigraphy as: Branch of stratigraphy dealing with the study of units of rock. Each unit is composed of a body of rock which is dominated by a certain lithology or similar color, mineralogic composition, and grain size.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 668

nodes.label: Paleoseismology
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Paleoseismology as: Branch of seismology concerned with ancient earthquakes. Clues which indicate seismic activities in the geologic past are used to date and determine the effects of those earthquakes.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 862

nodes.label: Quaternary
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Quaternary as: Period of geologic time approximately 2.6 million years ago extending to the present. In new studies, this term is deprecated in favor of Holocene and Pleistocene. https://doi.org/10.3133/fs20103059

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1657

nodes.label: Tertiary
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Tertiary as: Period of geologic time approximately 65 to 1.8 million years ago. In new studies, this term is deprecated in favor of Neogene and Paleogene. https://doi.org/10.3133/fs20103059

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1662

nodes.label: Cretaceous
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Cretaceous as: Period of geologic time approximately 145 to 65 million years ago. https://doi.org/10.3133/fs20103059

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1628

nodes.label: Jurassic

It includes the course of existence, the sum of experiences, the mode of existing, or the fact of being. Over the centuries inquiries into the nature of life have crossed the boundaries from philosophy to biology, forensic medicine, anthropology, etc., in creative as well as scientific literature. (Random House Unabridged Dictionary, 2d ed; Dr. James H. Cassedy, NLM History of Medicine Division)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D033302

nodes.label: Qi
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Qi as: The vital life force in the body, supposedly able to be regulated by acupuncture. It corresponds roughly to the Greek pneuma, the Latin spiritus, and the ancient Indian prana. The concept of life-breath or vital energy was formulated as an indication of the awareness of man, originally directed externally toward nature or society but later turned inward to the self or life within. (From Comparison between Concepts of Life-Breath in East and West, 15th International Symposium on the Comparative History of Medicine - East and West, August 26-September 3, 1990, Shizuoka, Japan, pp. ix-x)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D019413

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D014601

nodes.label: Vitalism
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Vitalism as: The metaphysical doctrine that the functions and processes of life are due to a vital principle distinct from physicochemical forces and that the laws of physics and chemistry alone cannot explain life functions and processes. Vitalism is opposed to mechanistic materialism. The belief was that matter was divided into two classes based on behavior with respect to heat: organic and inorganic. Inorganic material could be melted but could always be recovered by removing the heat source. Organic compounds changed form upon heating and could not be recovered by removing the heat source. The proposed explanation for the difference between organic and inorganic compounds was the Vitalism Theory, which stated that inorganic materials did not contain the vital force of life.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D014799

nodes.label: Yin-Yang
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Yin-Yang as: In Chinese philosophy and religion, two principles, one negative, dark, and feminine (yin) and one positive, bright, and masculine (yang), from whose interaction all things are produced and all things are dissolved. As a concept the two polar elements referred originally to the shady and sunny sides of a valley or a hill but it developed into the relationship of any contrasting pair: those specified above (female-male, etc.) as well as cold-hot, wet-dry, weak-strong, etc. It is not a distinct system of thought by itself but permeates Chinese life and thought. A balance of yin and yang is essential to health. A deficiency of either principle can manifest as disease. (Encyclopedia Americana)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D016709

Fuzzy logic plays a key role in many medical expert systems.

(From Stedman, 25th ed)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D004990

nodes.label: Empiricism
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Empiricism as: One of the principal schools of medical philosophy in ancient Greece and Rome. It developed in Alexandria between 270 and 220 B.C., the only one to have any success in reviving the essentials of the Hippocratic concept. The Empiricists declared that the search for ultimate causes of phenomena was vain, but they were active in endeavoring to discover immediate causes. The tripod of the Empirics was their own chance observations (experience), learning obtained from contemporaries and predecessors (experience of others), and, in the case of new diseases, the formation of conclusions from other diseases which they resembled (analogy). Empiricism enjoyed sporadic continuing popularity in later centuries up to the nineteenth. (From Castiglioni, A History of Medicine, 2d ed, p186; Dr. James H. Cassedy, NLM History of Medicine Division)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D019348

nodes.label: Holistic Health
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Holistic Health as: Health as viewed from the perspective that humans function as complete, integrated units rather than as aggregates of separate parts.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D006694

nodes.label: Humoralism
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Humoralism as: An ancient Greek medical theory that health and illness result from a balance or imbalance of body fluids or humors. The humors are blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D019364

nodes.label: Hygiene Hypothesis
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Hygiene Hypothesis as: The theory that infectious agents, symbiotic microorganisms, and parasites are normal stimulants for the maturation of the immune system toward a balanced immune response. The theory predicts that lack of such stimulation leads to allergies and AUTOIMMUNE DISEASES .

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D061148

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D004993

nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Holistic Nursing as: A philosophy of nursing practice that takes into account total patient care, considering the physical, emotional, social, economic, and spiritual needs of patients, their response to their illnesses, and the effect of illness on patients' abilities to meet self-care needs. (From Mosby's Medical, Nursing, & Allied Health Dictionary, 4th ed, p745)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D018939

(From Webster, 3d ed; American Heritage Dictionary, 2d college ed)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D002834

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D034682

nodes.label: Eastern Orthodoxy
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Eastern Orthodoxy as: The name given to the religion of the body of modern churches, including among others the Greek and Russian Orthodox, that is derived from the church of the Byzantine Empire, adheres to the Byzantine rite, and acknowledges the honorary primacy of the patriarch of Constantinople. (from American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language, 4th ed)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D033003

nodes.label: Protestantism

Protestant churches generally agree that the principle of authority should be the Scriptures rather than the institutional church or the pope. (from W.L. Reese, Dictionary of Philosophy and Religion, 1999)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D033303

nodes.label: Saints

This belief was most commonly held in religion and medicine of the medieval period and is also held in many tribal cultures today.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000067496

nodes.label: Spirituality

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D029181

nodes.label: Confucianism
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Confucianism as: A school of thought and set of moral, ethical, and political teachings usually considered to be founded by Confucius in 6th-5th century B.C. China. (from Cambridge Dictionary of Philosophy, 1995)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D032903

nodes.label: Mysticism
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Mysticism as: A philosophy based upon spiritual intuition that is believed to transcend ordinary sensory experiences or understanding.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D009228

nodes.label: Spiritualism
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Spiritualism as: Religious philosophy expressing the fundamental belief that departed spirits may be contacted by the living through a medium.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D013140

nodes.label: Yoga
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Yoga as: A major orthodox system of Hindu philosophy based on Sankhya (metaphysical dualism) but differing from it in being theistic and characterized by the teaching of raja-yoga as a practical method of liberating the self. It includes a system of exercises for attaining bodily or mental control and well-being with liberation of the self and union with the universal spirit. (From Webster, 3d ed)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D015013

nodes.label: Social Sciences
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Social Sciences as: Disciplines concerned with the interrelationships of individuals in a social environment including social organizations and institutions. Includes Sociology and Anthropology.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D012942

nodes.label: Environment Design
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Environment Design as: The structuring of the environment to permit or promote specific patterns of behavior.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D004779

nodes.label: Forecasting
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Forecasting as: The prediction or projection of the nature of future problems or existing conditions based upon the extrapolation or interpretation of existing scientific data or by the application of scientific methodology.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D005544

nodes.label: Government
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Government as: The complex of political institutions, laws, and customs through which the function of governing is carried out in a specific political unit.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D006076

nodes.label: Government Programs
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Government Programs as: Programs and activities sponsored or administered by local, state, or national governments.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D006078

nodes.label: Internationality
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Internationality as: The quality or state of relating to or affecting two or more nations. (After Merriam-Webster Collegiate Dictionary, 10th ed)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D038622

nodes.label: Policy
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Policy as: A course or method of action selected to guide and determine present and future decisions.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D057766

nodes.label: Political Systems
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Political Systems as: The units based on political theory and chosen by countries under which their governmental power is organized and administered to their citizens.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D011056

nodes.label: Politics
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Politics as: Activities concerned with governmental policies, functions, etc.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D011057

nodes.label: Private Sector
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Private Sector as: That distinct portion of the institutional, industrial, or economic structure of a country that is controlled or owned by non-governmental, private interests.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D017149

nodes.label: Public Sector
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Public Sector as: The area of a nation's economy that is tax-supported and under government control.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D017150

nodes.label: Quality of Life
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Quality of Life as: A generic concept reflecting concern with the modification and enhancement of life attributes, e.g., physical, political, moral, social environment as well as health and disease.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D011788

nodes.label: Work-Life Balance
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Work-Life Balance as: Complex ongoing balance between a person's working life and private life.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000072358

nodes.label: Anthropology, Medical
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Anthropology, Medical as: Field of social science that is concerned with differences between human groups as related to health status and beliefs.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D060432

nodes.label: Intersectional Framework
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Intersectional Framework as: Interconnections of social categorizations such as race, class, and gender, creating overlapping and interdependent systems of discrimination or disadvantage.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000091702

nodes.label: Media Exposure
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Media Exposure as: The extent to which individuals encounter messages and content via COMMUNICATION MEDIA.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000097822

nodes.label: Sociology, Medical
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Sociology, Medical as: The study of the social determinants and social effects of health and disease, and of the social structure of medical institutions or professions.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D012962

nodes.label: Crime
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Crime as: A violation of the criminal law, i.e., a breach of the conduct code specifically sanctioned by the state, which through its administrative agencies prosecutes offenders and imposes and administers punishments. The concept includes unacceptable actions whether prosecuted or going unpunished.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D003415

nodes.label: Criminal Law
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Criminal Law as: A branch of law that defines criminal offenses, regulates the apprehension, charging and trial of suspected persons, and fixes the penalties and modes of treatment applicable to convicted offenders.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D003416

nodes.label: Forensic Sciences
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Forensic Sciences as: Disciplines that apply sciences to law. Forensic sciences include a wide range of disciplines, such as FORENSIC TOXICOLOGY ; FORENSIC ANTHROPOLOGY ; FORENSIC MEDICINE ; FORENSIC DENTISTRY ; and others.
