nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Affect as: The feeling-tone accompaniment of an idea or mental representation. It is the most direct psychic derivative of instinct and the psychic representative of the various bodily changes by means of which instincts manifest themselves.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000339

nodes.label: Anger
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Anger as: A strong emotional feeling of displeasure aroused by being interfered with, injured or threatened.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000786

nodes.label: Anxiety
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Anxiety as: Feelings or emotions of dread, apprehension, and impending disaster but not disabling as with ANXIETY DISORDERS .

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D001007

nodes.label: Apathy
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Apathy as: Lack of emotion or emotional expression; a disorder of motivation that persists over time.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D057565

nodes.label: Bereavement
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Bereavement as: Refers to the whole process of grieving and mourning and is associated with a deep sense of loss and sadness.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D001601

nodes.label: Boredom
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Boredom as: A psychological state resulting from any activity that lacks motivation, or from enforced continuance in an uninteresting situation.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D001887

nodes.label: Courage
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Courage as: State of mind or spirit that enables one to act in the face of perceived danger, difficulty, or pain.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D066279

nodes.label: Depression
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Depression as: Depressive states usually of moderate intensity in contrast with MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER present in neurotic and psychotic disorders.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D003863

nodes.label: Disgust
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Disgust as: A feeling of revulsion or strong disapproval aroused by something unpleasant or offensive.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000078382

nodes.label: Emotional Exhaustion
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Emotional Exhaustion as: A state of feeling emotionally overextended and drained.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000097815

nodes.label: Bioethical Issues
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Bioethical Issues as: Clusters of topics that fall within the domain of BIOETHICS , the field of study concerned with value questions that arise in biomedicine and health care delivery.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D026688

nodes.label: Bioethics
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Bioethics as: A branch of applied ethics that studies the value implications of practices and developments in life sciences, medicine, and health care.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D001675

nodes.label: Codes of Ethics
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Codes of Ethics as: Systematic statements of principles or rules of appropriate professional conduct, usually established by professional societies.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D032781

nodes.label: Complicity
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Complicity as: Association with or participation in an act that is, or is perceived to be, criminal or immoral. One is complicitous when one promotes or unduly benefits from practices or institutions that are morally or legally suspect.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D028661

nodes.label: Conflict of Interest
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Conflict of Interest as: A situation in which an individual might benefit personally from official or professional actions. It includes a conflict between a person's private interests and official responsibilities in a position of trust. The term is not restricted to government officials. The concept refers both to actual conflict of interest and the appearance or perception of conflict.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D016265

nodes.label: Double Effect Principle
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Double Effect Principle as: Guideline for determining when it is morally permissible to perform an action to pursue a good end with knowledge that the action will also bring about bad results. It generally states that, in cases where a contemplated action has such double effect, the action is permissible only if: it is not wrong in itself; the bad result is not intended; the good result is not a direct causal result of the bad result; and the good result is proportionate to the bad result. (from Solomon, Double Effect, in Becker, The Encyclopedia of Ethics, 1992)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D034723

nodes.label: Ethical Analysis
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ethical Analysis as: The use of systematic methods of ethical examination, such as CASUISTRY or ETHICAL THEORY , in reasoning about moral problems.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D026689

nodes.label: Ethical Relativism
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ethical Relativism as: The philosophical view that conceptions of truth and moral values are not absolute but are relative to the persons or groups holding them. (from American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language, 4th ed)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D028781

nodes.label: Ethical Review
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ethical Review as: A formal process of examination of patient care or research proposals for conformity with ethical standards. The review is usually conducted by an organized clinical or research ethics committee ( CLINICAL ETHICS COMMITTEES or RESEARCH ETHICS COMMITTEES ), sometimes by a subset of such a committee, an ad hoc group, or an individual ethicist ( ETHICISTS ).

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D026724

nodes.label: Ethical Theory
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ethical Theory as: A philosophically coherent set of propositions (for example, utilitarianism) which attempts to provide general norms for the guidance and evaluation of moral conduct. (from Beauchamp and Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics, 4th ed)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D028663

nodes.label: Ethics, Business
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ethics, Business as: The moral obligations governing the conduct of commercial or industrial enterprises.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D040861

nodes.label: Ethics, Institutional
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ethics, Institutional as: The moral and ethical obligations or responsibilities of institutions.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D004991

nodes.label: Ethics, Professional
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ethics, Professional as: The principles of proper conduct concerning the rights and duties of the professional, relations with patients or consumers and fellow practitioners, as well as actions of the professional and interpersonal relations with patient or consumer families. (From Stedman, 25th ed)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D004995

nodes.label: Ethics, Research
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ethics, Research as: The moral obligations governing the conduct of research. Used for discussions of research ethics as a general topic.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D032984

nodes.label: Humanism
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Humanism as: An ethical system which emphasizes human values and the personal worth of each individual, as well as concern for the dignity and freedom of humankind.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D006808

nodes.label: Moral Status
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Moral Status as: A philosophical description of intrinsic self-worth and dignity which bestows basic rights of life, liberty, and freedom from harm.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000072577

nodes.label: Personhood
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Personhood as: The state or condition of being a human individual accorded moral and/or legal rights. Criteria to be used to determine this status are subject to debate, and range from the requirement of simply being a human organism to such requirements as that the individual be self-aware and capable of rational thought and moral agency.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D028723

nodes.label: Principle-Based Ethics
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Principle-Based Ethics as: An approach to ethics that focuses on theories of the importance of general principles such as respect for autonomy, beneficence/nonmaleficence, and justice.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D028662

nodes.label: Symbolic Interactionism
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Symbolic Interactionism as: Theoretical approach to social processes with a fundamental concern with power phenomena. There is a focus on the analysis of culture, the influence of Foucault, and the development of feminist perspectives.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000073624

nodes.label: Ethics, Clinical
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ethics, Clinical as: The identification, analysis, and resolution of moral problems that arise in the care of patients. (Bioethics Thesaurus)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D026690

nodes.label: Casuistry
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Casuistry as: A method of ETHICAL ANALYSIS that emphasizes practical problem solving through examining individual cases that are considered to be representative; sometimes used to denote specious argument or rationalization. Differentiate from casuistics, which is the recording and study of cases and disease.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D032764

nodes.label: Retrospective Moral Judgment
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Retrospective Moral Judgment as: The application of current standards of morality to past actions, institutions, or persons.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D035481

nodes.label: Wedge Argument
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Wedge Argument as: An assertion that an action apparently unobjectionable in itself would set in motion a train of events leading ultimately to an undesirable outcome. (From Cambridge Dictionary of Philosophy, 1995)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D035761

nodes.label: Ethics Consultation
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Ethics Consultation as: Services provided by an individual ethicist ( ETHICISTS ) or an ethics team or committee ( ETHICS COMMITTEES, CLINICAL ) to address the ethical issues involved in a specific clinical case. The central purpose is to improve the process and outcomes of patients' care by helping to identify, analyze, and resolve ethical problems.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D033061

nodes.label: Professionalism
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Professionalism as: The level of skill, good judgment, and polite behavior expected from people trained to do their jobs well.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000068616

nodes.label: Therapeutic Equipoise
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Therapeutic Equipoise as: Expectation of real uncertainty on the part of the investigator regarding the comparative therapeutic merits of each arm in a trial.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D057212

nodes.label: Therapeutic Misconception
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Therapeutic Misconception as: Misunderstanding among individuals, frequently research subjects, of scientific methods such as randomization and placebo controls.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D055990

nodes.label: Feminism
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Feminism as: The theory of the political, economic, and social equality of the sexes and organized activity on behalf of women's rights and interests. (Webster New Collegiate Dictionary, 1981)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D019513

nodes.label: Beneficence
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Beneficence as: The state or quality of being kind, charitable, or beneficial. (from American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language, 4th ed). The ethical principle of BENEFICENCE requires producing net benefit over harm. (Bioethics Thesaurus)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D026686

nodes.label: Personal Autonomy
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Personal Autonomy as: Self-directing freedom and especially moral independence. An ethical principle holds that the autonomy of persons ought to be respected. (Bioethics Thesaurus)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D026684

nodes.label: Social Justice
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Social Justice as: An interactive process whereby members of a community are concerned for the equality and rights of all.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D012935

nodes.label: Environmental Justice
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Environmental Justice as: The fair treatment and meaningful involvement of all people regardless of race, color, national origin, or income, with respect to the development, implementation, and enforcement of environmental laws, regulations, and policies. (www.epa.gov/environmentaljustice/learn-about-environmental-justice)

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000091383

nodes.label: Moral Obligations
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Moral Obligations as: Duties that are based in ETHICS , rather than in law.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D028681

nodes.label: Relational Autonomy
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Relational Autonomy as: The social context within which all individuals exist and acknowledge the emotional and embodied aspects of decision-makers. The approach acknowledges the central role of others in decision-making, including clinicians, who have a responsibility to engage patients’ and surrogates’ emotional experiences.

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000080105

nodes.label: Antiracism
nodes.summary: NLM MeSH describes Antiracism as: Beliefs, actions or intentions, and policies that oppose RACISM or discrimination based on RACE .

sources.title: NLM MeSH Browser descriptor D000095026

nodes.label: Biological and physical processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Biological and physical processes as: All continuing activities, functions, and phenomena associated with organisms and non-living matter. This category is also used for bioenergetic processes

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 101

nodes.label: Water properties
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Water properties as: Measurable physical and chemical characteristics of water from different sources.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1304

nodes.label: Natural resources
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Natural resources as: Stocks of anything naturally occurring that have a beneficial use for man including economic, nutritional, recreational, aesthetic, and other benefits.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 777

nodes.label: Atmospheric and climatic processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Atmospheric and climatic processes as: Phenomena affecting or occurring within the mass of gases that surrounds the earth, including its physics, chemistry, dynamics, and weather conditions. This category is also used for climate , microclimate , weather , with field inventory and monitoring for weather monitoring , and with field inventory and monitoring for weather observations

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 63

nodes.label: Coastal processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Coastal processes as: Processes unique to coastal areas including longshore transport, beach erosion, storm surge, shoreline change, delta formation, barrier island migration, beach stabilization by vegetation This category is also used with erosion for beach erosion , with erosion for coastal erosion , with hazards for coastal hazards , shoreline change , with erosion for shoreline erosion , and with erosion for shoreline retreat

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1799

nodes.label: Ecological processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Ecological processes as: Dynamic biogeochemical interactions that occur among and between biotic and abiotic components of the biosphere. This category is also used for ecological models and environmental processes

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 310

nodes.label: Estuarine processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Estuarine processes as: Processes affecting estuaries including tides, waves, mixing of fluvial and marine waters This category is also used with sediment transport for estuarine sediment transport

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1800

nodes.label: Evolution
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Evolution as: Change in the genetic composition of populations of living organisms. This category is also used for gene flow

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1702

nodes.label: Fires
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Fires as: Combustion, marked by heat, light, flames, and often, smoke, caused by the natural or human-induced ignition of flammable materials. For fires set as part of natural resource management, use controlled fires. This category is also used with hazard preparedness for fire preparedness and fires (uncontrolled)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 384

nodes.label: Geochemical processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Geochemical processes as: Processes affecting the amount, distribution, or structure of chemical elements in air, water, soil, rocks, and minerals.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 435

nodes.label: Geologic processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Geologic processes as: All types of processes involving geological structures. This category is also used for lithification

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 451

nodes.label: Hydrocarbon reservoir processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Hydrocarbon reservoir processes as: Interactions among groundwater, hydrocarbons, and rock properties of subsurface geological formations, affecting the potential of those formations to form, trap, and permit the passage and extraction of hydrocarbons.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2295

nodes.label: Impact cratering
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Impact cratering as: Impact of extraterrestrial objects such as asteroids, comets, and meteorites on Earth. This category is also used for asteroid impact , bolide impact , comet impact , and meteor impact

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1718

nodes.label: Ocean processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Ocean processes as: Recurrent natural changes that are physical, biological, or chemical, actively affecting the seas and oceans. This category is also used with sediment transport for marine sediment transport , with hazards for ocean hazards , and with ocean characteristics for oceans

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 816

nodes.label: Physiological processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Physiological processes as: Characteristics and processes of individual organisms that are not the direct result of their interaction with other organisms or with the environment.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1347

nodes.label: Dissolved gases
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Dissolved gases as: Gases such as ammonia, oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide in solution measured in a water sample.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1682

nodes.label: Dissolved metals
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Dissolved metals as: Metal elements in solution, of concern in studies of hazards such as mine drainage and of water resource usability.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1999

nodes.label: Dissolved organic compounds
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Dissolved organic compounds as: Organic compounds present in water, typically as anthropogenic contaminants including pharmaceuticals, pesticides, and herbicides.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2000

nodes.label: Nutrient content (water)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Nutrient content (water) as: Contaminants in water that nourish organisms, especially plants. Includes nitrogen and phosphorus, either of which can lead to the harmful growth of algae and other plants when present to excess in a body of water. This category is also used for nitrogen content and phosphorus content

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 806

nodes.label: Oxygen content (water)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Oxygen content (water) as: Measurement of the concentration of oxygen dissolved in water, which is an important indicator of the condition of a water body. This category is also used for anoxia , dissolved oxygen , and hypoxia

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 854

nodes.label: Salinity
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Salinity as: Measure of the concentration of salts dissolved in a solution. This category is also used for chloride concentration

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1010

nodes.label: Sound velocity
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Sound velocity as: Estimates of the velocity of sound in water, indexed by depth at a specific location, usually calculated from other water properties. This category is also used with profiles for sound velocity profiles

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2080

nodes.label: Suspended material (water)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Suspended material (water) as: Sediment or organic material carried in suspension in the water column, in contrast to material that moves on or near the bottom. May be measured directly by sampling, or indirectly by acoustic or optical backscatter or transmission. This category is also used for suspended sediment concentration and suspended-sediment concentration

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1129

nodes.label: Water column reflectivity
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Water column reflectivity as: A measure of the strength of reflection from small particles suspended in water. It is usually measured by sending a pulse of sound or light through the water and measuring the sound or light that is returned. Water column reflectivity can be used to measure the concentration of suspended particles. This category is also used for backscatter (water column) , water column acoustic reflectivity , and water column optical reflectivity

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2264

nodes.label: Water hardness
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Water hardness as: Indicator of the concentration of alkaline salts in water, mainly calcium and magnesium, as a measure of water quality. This category is also used for hardness (water)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1301

nodes.label: Water pH
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Water pH as: The negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration or activity of a water solution. Used for expressing both acidity (pH less than 7) and alkalinity (pH greater than 7), with 7 considered neutral. This category is also used for pH (water)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1302

nodes.label: Water temperature
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Water temperature as: The degrees of heat of water from a given source at a specific time. This category is also used for temperature (water)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1312

nodes.label: Energy resources
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Energy resources as: Natural resources that are used for heat and power generation, including oil, natural gas, coal, and geothermal energy. This category is also used for energy sources and fossil fuels

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 799

nodes.label: Fishery resources
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Fishery resources as: The stock of anadromous, marine, and freshwater fish in fishing areas of commercial, subsistence, and recreational value.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 391

nodes.label: Forest resources
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Forest resources as: Trees and associated vegetation available for human use. Use for timber and other forest resources with economic value. This category is also used for forestry

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 411

nodes.label: Mineral resources
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Mineral resources as: Natural occurrences of useful inorganic elements or compounds.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 745

nodes.label: Soil resources
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Soil resources as: Natural resources of unconsolidated fragmented rock, humus, and mineral matter that cover the surface of the earth. This category is also used with contamination and pollution for soil pollution

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1080

nodes.label: Water resources
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Water resources as: Stocks of water, the liquid derived from precipitation. A constituent of living matter and necessity for all life, it covers a large proportion of the earth's surface. This category is also used for hydrosphere and with contamination and pollution for water pollution

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1308

nodes.label: Atmospheric circulation
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Atmospheric circulation as: Movement of atmospheric gases around the earth.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 64

nodes.label: Atmospheric deposition (chemical & particulate)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Atmospheric deposition (chemical & particulate) as: The transfer of substances from the air to the surface of the earth, either in wet form (rain, fog, snow, dew, frost, hail) or in dry form (gases, aerosols, particles). This category is also used for atmospheric deposition (chemical and particulate) and atmospheric dust deposition

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 66

nodes.label: Climate change
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Climate change as: Long-term alteration in the characteristic weather conditions of a region, such as changes in precipitation and temperature. This category is also used for climate history , climate variability , climatic change , global climate change , global warming , and paleoclimate

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 168

nodes.label: Droughts
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Droughts as: Extended periods of moisture deficit over a sizeable area sufficient to have an adverse effect on vegetation, animals, or man. This category is also used for drought

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 284

nodes.label: Evaporation
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Evaporation as: Transfer of water from a surface into the atmosphere. This category is also used with transpiration for evapotranspiration

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1355

nodes.label: Greenhouse effect
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Greenhouse effect as: Local, regional, or global warming in the atmosphere due to the higher heat capacity of certain gases such as carbon dioxide, methane, and ozone.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1704

nodes.label: Ocean-atmosphere interaction
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Ocean-atmosphere interaction as: Processes, including momentum, heat, gas and other exchanges, which result in profound effects on climate and interactions between the air in the lowest part of the atmosphere and the oceans. This category is also used for El Nino and La Nina

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 823

nodes.label: Precipitation (atmospheric)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Precipitation (atmospheric) as: Any or all forms of water particles that fall from the atmosphere, such as rain, snow, hail and sleet. This category is also used with field inventory and monitoring for precipitation measurement , rain , rainfall , with field inventory and monitoring for rainfall measurement , snow , snowfall , and with field inventory and monitoring for snowfall measurement

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 927

nodes.label: Storms
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Storms as: Atmospheric disturbances with winds of unusual force or direction. Accompanied by rain, snow, hail, or sleet, and often by thunder and lightning.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1102

nodes.label: Wind
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Wind as: Local air movements. This category is also used with erosion for wind erosion

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1690

nodes.label: Barrier island migration
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Barrier island migration as: The slow, landward movement of barrier islands in response to sea level rise and repeated storm washover.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2069

nodes.label: Coastal emergence
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Coastal emergence as: Relative uplift of the coast accompanied by seaward displacement of the shoreline. This category is also used for regression (marine)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2070

nodes.label: Coastal submergence
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Coastal submergence as: Relative subsidence of the coast accompanied by landward displacement of the shoreline. This category is also used for transgression (marine)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2071

nodes.label: Longshore currents
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Longshore currents as: Movement of water parallel to the coast due to waves striking the shoreline at an angle This category is also used with sediment transport for littoral drift and with sediment transport for longshore drift

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1801

nodes.label: Shoreline accretion
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Shoreline accretion as: Seaward migration of the shoreline resulting from the addition of earth materials.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2072

nodes.label: Tidal currents
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Tidal currents as: Currents caused by tidal changes in water level from one body of water to another.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2068

nodes.label: Algal blooms
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Algal blooms as: Exceptional growth of algae and cyanobacteria in lakes, rivers or oceans due to excessive nutrients or climatic conditions. This category is also used for brown tides , with hazards for harmful algal blooms , and red tides

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 30

nodes.label: Bioaccumulation
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Bioaccumulation as: The biological sequestering of a substance at a higher concentration than that at which it occurs in the surrounding environment or medium. Also, the process whereby a substance enters an organism through the gills, epithelial tissues, dietary, or other sources. This category is also used for bioconcentration

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 88

nodes.label: Biogeochemical cycling
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Biogeochemical cycling as: The cycling of chemical constituents through a biological system. This category is also used for biogeochemical functioning , biogeochemical processes , decomposition (organic) , and organic decomposition

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 93

nodes.label: Biological productivity
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Biological productivity as: The rate at which primary producers in the ecosystem utilize solar energy to produce food for consumption by other organisms. Do not use this term for productivity of organisms related to studies of the reproduction rates of a species.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 108

nodes.label: Carbon flux
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Carbon flux as: The rate and amount of carbon exchanged between the oceans, atmosphere, land, and living things. This category is also used for carbon exchange

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2277

nodes.label: Contaminant transport
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Contaminant transport as: Processes involved in the movement of impurities through air, water, and soil.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 196

nodes.label: Dispersal (organisms)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Dispersal (organisms) as: The dissemination or geographic spread of individuals of a plant or animal population. This category is also used for colonization (organisms)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 268

nodes.label: Ecological competition
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Ecological competition as: The struggle between members of two or more species for scarce environmental resources.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 308

nodes.label: Ecosystem functions
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Ecosystem functions as: The total life activities of organisms in habitats and the effects of those activities on the nonliving components of the environment. This category is also used with estuarine ecosystems for estuarine ecosystem functions

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 315

nodes.label: Ecosystem resilience
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Ecosystem resilience as: Measure of the persistence of systems and of their ability to absorb change and disturbance and still maintain the same relationships between populations or state variables. (Holling, 1973) This category is also used for ecological resilience

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2281

nodes.label: Eutrophication
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Eutrophication as: The process by which water becomes enriched with plant nutrients, most commonly phosphorus and nitrogen.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 359

nodes.label: Extinction and extirpation
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Extinction and extirpation as: Extinction is the complete disappearance of a species from the earth. Extirpation is the complete disappearance (elimination) of a species from a given region, island, or area. This category is also used for extirpation

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 365

nodes.label: Habitat alteration and disturbance
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Habitat alteration and disturbance as: Changes in the environments where plants and animals live. Includes natural changes as well as results of human actions, deliberate or accidental. This category is also used for ecological disturbance , environmental disturbance , habitat destruction , and habitat disturbance

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 522

nodes.label: Migration (organisms)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Migration (organisms) as: The movement of animals, often periodical, from one area to another due to seasonal changes, availability of food, or climatic conditions. This category is also used with invasive species for biological invasions , with biogeography for flyways , and seasonal migration

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 743

nodes.label: Pollination
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Pollination as: Wind, bees, or other agents transfer plant pollen from flower anthers or cones to stigmas, thereby fertilizing plants for reproduction.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 915

nodes.label: Succession (biological)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Succession (biological) as: Gradual replacement of one species in an area by another. This category is also used for ecologic succession

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1123

nodes.label: Transpiration
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Transpiration as: Evaporation of water from plants. This category is also used with evaporation for evapotranspiration

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1356

nodes.label: Estuarine currents
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Estuarine currents as: Movement of water within estuaries due to the complex interaction of winds, tides, and variations in water density

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1802

nodes.label: Estuarine mixing
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Estuarine mixing as: Interaction of tidal forcing and river discharge in an estuary, leading to any of three vertical salinity profiles: salt wedge, stratified, or well mixed. We also include mixing due to extreme events such as storm surge.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1803

nodes.label: Wildfires
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Wildfires as: Uncontrolled fires that originate as a result of natural phenomena or human activities in natural areas such as forests, grasslands, or shrub lands, but may also spread to structures and human-occupied environments. This category is also used for wildland fire

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2305

nodes.label: Biodegradation
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Biodegradation as: Reduction in the concentration of harmful chemicals by the action of animals and plants. This category is also used for natural attenuation (harmful chemicals)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1346

nodes.label: Carbon sequestration
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Carbon sequestration as: Long-term storage of carbon in soils and terrestrial organic material, either by natural or engineered processes. Typically of importance for the balance of CO2 in the global climate system. This category is also used for carbon capture , carbon capture and storage , and carbon storage

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1731

nodes.label: Ocean acidification
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Ocean acidification as: Decrease in the pH of ocean waters as a result of the increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2058

nodes.label: Ore formation
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Ore formation as: Geochemical processes resulting in concentration of useful chemical elements and compounds, in earth materials. Typically refers to metal ores. This category is also used for metallogenesis , metallogeny , and mineralization

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1703

nodes.label: Oxidation and reduction
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Oxidation and reduction as: Addition or reduction of oxygen in a compound accompanied by exchange of electrons among atoms. This category is also used for fermentation

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1708

nodes.label: Reaction transport
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Reaction transport as: Chemical reactions occurring during ground-water flow.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1711

nodes.label: Sorption
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Sorption as: Attachment of chemical substances to materials, either externally (by adsorption) or internally (by absorption). This category is also used for absorption and adsorption

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1715

nodes.label: Thermal maturation
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Thermal maturation as: Chemical alteration of organic material within sediments and sedimentary rocks as a result of heat. Measures of thermal maturation indicate the extent of transformation of detrital organic material into coal and petroleum. This category is also used for thermal indices , thermal maturity , and vitrinite reflectance

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2279

nodes.label: Deformation (geologic)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Deformation (geologic) as: Change in form and structure of geologic materials in response to stress, typically heat and pressure. This category is also used for rheology and strain history

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1699

nodes.label: Diagenesis
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Diagenesis as: Chemical, physical, and biological changes in sediment during and after its conversion to rock (lithification).

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 248

nodes.label: Earth tides
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Earth tides as: Periodic changes in the earth surface topography caused by the gravitational attraction of the moon and sun, measured with tiltmeters. Used in studies of volcanic activity.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1683

nodes.label: Earthquakes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Earthquakes as: Ground shaking caused by the sudden release of accumulated strain by an abrupt shift of rock along a fracture in the earth or by volcanic or magmatic activity, or other sudden stress changes in the earth. This category is also used with hazards for earthquake hazards

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 304

nodes.label: Erosion
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Erosion as: The process whereby materials of the earth's crust are loosened, dissolved, or worn away and simultaneously moved from one place to another. This category is also used with coastal processes for beach erosion , with coastal processes for coastal erosion , dissolution , with coastal processes for shoreline erosion , with coastal processes for shoreline retreat , and with wind for wind erosion

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 353

nodes.label: Fluid migration
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Fluid migration as: Movement or migration of fluids, including petroleum and other chemicals through earth materials by natural or anthropogenic forces. This category is also used for interstitial fluid and pore fluid

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 2282

nodes.label: Glaciation
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Glaciation as: The geologic processes involved in the formation, movement, changes, and effects of large ice masses (glaciers).

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 482

nodes.label: Heat flow (earth)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Heat flow (earth) as: Energy transferred by a difference in temperature through the surface of the earth. This category is also used for geothermics and heatflow (earth)

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 534

nodes.label: Hydrothermal processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Hydrothermal processes as: Natural phenomena relating to heated water generated by igneous activity.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 562

nodes.label: Isostasy
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Isostasy as: Condition of equilibrium or buoyancy of the earth's crust above the mantle.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 608

nodes.label: Magnetic storms
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Magnetic storms as: A period of time during which the earth's magnetic field varies rapidly. During magnetic storms, satellite electronics can be damaged through the build up and subsequent discharge of static electric charges and astronauts and high-altitude pilots can be subjected to increased levels of radiation. This category is also used for geomagnetic storms

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1721

nodes.label: Metamorphism (geological)
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Metamorphism (geological) as: Process by which rocks are altered in composition and texture by extreme heat, high pressure, or the action of chemicals.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 727

nodes.label: Sediment transport
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Sediment transport as: Transport of solid particles of unconsolidated rock and mineral fragments, chemical precipitates, or biological materials. This category is also used for alluvial transport , bed load , bedload , density flow , dust transport , with estuarine processes for estuarine sediment transport , with longshore currents for littoral drift , with longshore currents for longshore drift , with ocean processes for marine sediment transport , suspended load , and turbidity flow

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1034

nodes.label: Sedimentation
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Sedimentation as: Process of deposition of sediments (loose, uncemented pieces of rock, mineral fragments, or biological materials). The sediments settle out of water or air into layers on a surface. This category is also used for alluvial sedimentation , deposition (sediment) , and dust deposition

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1036

nodes.label: Slope processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Slope processes as: The down slope movement of earth material under the influence of gravity. This category is also used for mass wasting and soil creep

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1736

nodes.label: Soil formation
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Soil formation as: Geological, geochemical, and ecological processes that work together to produce soils. This category is also used for pedogenesis

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1710

nodes.label: Subsidence
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Subsidence as: Settling, compaction, or caving in of land caused by subsurface mining, ground-water withdrawal, or pumping of oil and gas. This category is also used for land subsidence and with maps and atlases for land subsidence maps

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 624

nodes.label: Tectonic processes
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Tectonic processes as: The structural forces affecting the deformation, uplift, and movement of the earth's crust. This category is also used for continental drift , dynamic geology , with maps and atlases for paleotectonic maps , plate tectonics , subduction , with maps and atlases for tectonic maps , tectonics , and wilson cycle

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1145

nodes.label: Uplift
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Uplift as: Local or regional rise in the elevation of the land surface, usually due to tectonic or volcanic processes.

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1751

nodes.label: Volcanic activity
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Volcanic activity as: Episodes during which gases, ash, and lava (molten rock) escape from vents in the earth's crust, accompanied by minor tremors. This category is also used for eruption , lava flows , pyroclastic flows , volcanic tremors , volcanism , and with field inventory and monitoring for volcano monitoring

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1286

nodes.label: Floods
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Floods as: Relatively high water that overflows the natural or artificial banks of a stream or coastal area that submerges land not normally below water level. This category is also used for bankfull stage and with hazard preparedness for flood preparedness

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 398

nodes.label: Groundwater and surface-water interaction
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Groundwater and surface-water interaction as: Traditionally, management of water resources has focused on surface water or groundwater as if they were separate entities. As development of land and water resources increases, it is apparent that development of either of these resources affects the quantity and quality of the other. Nearly all surface-water features (streams, lakes, reservoirs, wetlands, and estuaries) interact with groundwater. These interactions take many forms. In many situations, surface-water bodies gain water and solutes from groundwater systems and in others the surface-water body is a source of groundwater recharge and causes changes in groundwater quality. As a result, withdrawal of water from streams can deplete groundwater or conversely, pumpage of groundwater can deplete water in streams, lakes, or wetlands. Pollution of surface water can cause degradation of groundwater quality and conversely pollution of groundwater can degrade surface water. This category is also used for aquifer-surface water interaction , ground-water/surface-water interaction , groundwater/surface water interaction , hyporheic zone processes , surface water/groundwater interaction , and surface-water/ground-water interaction

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 1692

nodes.label: Groundwater flow
nodes.summary: The USGS Thesaurus defines Groundwater flow as: Movement of subsurface water in the saturated zone from areas of recharge to areas of discharge. This category is also used for ground-water flow , groundwater flow modeling , and groundwater movement

sources.title: USGS Thesaurus term 514

support.quote:
Title:
A Spin Entanglement Witness for Quantum Gravity
[Submitted on 19 Jul 2017]

Here, we introduce an idea for such a test based on the principle that two objects cannot be entangled without a quantum mediator. We show that despite the weakness of gravity, the phase evolution induced by the gravitational interaction of two micron size test masses in adjacent matter-wave interferometers can detectably entangle them even when they are placed far apart enough to keep Casimir-Polder forces at bay. We provide a prescription for witnessing this entanglement, which certifies gravity as a quantum coherent mediator, through simple correlation measurements between two spins: one embedded in each test mass.

Subjects:
Quantum Physics (quant-ph)
; General Relativity and Quantum Cosmology (gr-qc); High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

Title:

We report results of a search for nuclear recoils induced by weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter using the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) two-phase xenon time projection chamber. This analysis uses a total exposure of $4.2\pm0.1$ tonne-years from 280 live days of LZ operation, of which $3.3\pm0.1$ tonne-years and 220 live days are new.

scope.uncertainty: Proposed reinterpretation of at least some masses; no claim applying to all barite occurrences

support.quote: However, new observations suggest that at least some of these barite masses represent the mineralized remnants of terrestrial hot spring pools and associated shallow subsurface hydrothermal plumbing.

These barite masses occur at the uppermost tips of hydrothermal feeder veins along faults (that is, hydrothermal fluid conduits), and some are found immediately beneath overlying strata with known geyserite and siliceous sinter deposits.

support.quote:
The cause of the Cit
−
lineage’s extinction remains unknown. We have rejected our initial hypothesis that on-going adaptation of the Cit
+
bacteria caused the extinction. A purely stochastic extinction of the Cit
−
lineage is also extremely unlikely.

We propose, therefore, that the cause of the Cit
−
extinction was a “random catastrophe”, that is, a large, rare event that reduced the size of the Ara–3 population as a whole or, at least, the Cit
−
lineage within it. We do not know the nature of this random catastrophe, but it could have been some unusual variation in laboratory conditions, such as soap residue in a flask or a problem with the deionized water used to make the culture medium.

decisions.rationale: The retained Leon passage locates rudimentary citrate utilization in Ara−3 after 31,500 LTEE generations and more complete citrate use in its descendants by 33,000. The summary attributes the chronology to the authors and distinguishes Cit+ from Cit++; claim kind, life domain, neutral metadata, and independent node identity fit. No relationship or taxonomy placement is proposed.
decisions.limitations: This is a historical report, not direct observation of the first Cit+ cell, and it cannot establish similar changes in the other eleven populations.

decisions.rationale: The retained Leon et al. (2018) source explicitly identifies the Ara−3 LTEE population, reports emergence of citrate utilization after 31,500 generations, and distinguishes this initial phenotype from descendants able to fully exploit citrate by 33,000 generations. The claim's identity, label, life domain, kind and bounded chronology are justified. Status reported attributes the historical account to its source; undated and frontier=false make no positive chronology-classification or currency assertion. No identity merge, taxonomy placement or graph relation is proposed.
decisions.limitations: The first successful Cit+ cell was not directly observed. The historical chronology does not establish identical evolution in the other eleven LTEE populations. The other retained source captures do not supply additional independent evidence for this assertion.

decisions.rationale: Leon reports a 2.2% competitive fitness advantage for ZDB564 versus its Cit− revertant ZDB706 attributable to the citT-activating duplication. The complete label, strains, effect, life-domain claim representation, and reported/undated/frontier=false metadata match the source.
decisions.limitations: The estimate is specific to this evolved background and assay, not proof that citT activation generally increases fitness.

decisions.rationale: Leon et al. directly report a 2.2% competitive fitness advantage associated with the citT-activating duplication in ZDB564 relative to its Cit− revertant ZDB706. Both strain identities and the measured effect are preserved. The life-domain claim node represents one specific experimental result, with neutral scientific metadata and no unsupported relationship or placement.
decisions.limitations: The comparison applies to this evolved genetic background and DM-medium competition assay. Arabinose-marker controls address a potential experimental confound but do not establish that activating citT universally increases fitness. The advantage should not be conflated with the later Cit++ refinement phenotype.

decisions.rationale: The REL606 engineered P_rnk-citT versus null-cassette assay directly reports a 1.0% advantage with one-tailed P=0.033 and n=12, described as weak evidence near assay precision. The candidate explicitly calls the activation engineered, and its kind, domain, neutral metadata and independent identity are justified.
decisions.limitations: The knock-in mimics but is not the original tandem duplication; neither a robust benefit nor actual Cit+ evolution in the ancestor is established.

decisions.rationale: The source reports an engineered P_rnk-citT knock-in comparison in ancestral strain REL606, a measured 1.0% fitness advantage, one-tailed P=0.033 and n=12. It explicitly characterizes the statistical evidence as relatively weak because the effect approaches assay resolution. The canonical summary preserves both the engineering intervention and uncertainty; claim kind, life domain, independent identity and neutral metadata are justified.
decisions.limitations: A chromosomal knock-in mimicking citT activation is not the naturally evolved rnk-citG tandem duplication. The result does not show that Cit+ spontaneously evolved in ancestral REL606, that the advantage was robust, or that it was sufficient to survive competition against alternative beneficial mutations.

decisions.rationale: Leon reports disadvantageous citT activation in 11 of 23 additional evolved pre-Cit+ clones, including five losses exceeding 20%. The sampled population, numerical counts, claim label, life domain, neutral representation, and lack of proposed graph edges are appropriate.
decisions.limitations: The result uses selected clones and statistical tests; it cannot be generalized to all genetic backgrounds or other LTEE populations.

decisions.rationale: Leon et al. describe testing 23 additional evolved pre-Cit+ clones and report a competitive disadvantage following citT activation in 11, including five disadvantages greater than 20%, evaluated using one-tailed bootstrap tests. The candidate retains the sampled-clone denominator, direction of the effect and distinction between rudimentary Cit+ and refined Cit++. Claim kind, life domain, identity, standalone placement and neutral metadata are appropriate.
decisions.limitations: The 23 clones are a selected sample from one LTEE population, not all historical genetic backgrounds. Fitness effects may depend on private mutations and environmental conditions. The experiments do not prove that every possible route to citrate utilization was inaccessible in those backgrounds.

decisions.rationale: The authors explicitly report the pooled −5.4% estimate and [−7.2%, −3.6%] interval for ZDB425, ZDB458 and ZDB464. The record confines interpretation to the tested intermediate phylogenetic group, with the named isolates and lineage caveats.
decisions.limitations: The authors allow for unobserved changes between sampled generations; the responsible mutations are not experimentally identified by this estimate.

decisions.rationale: The retained phylogenetic analysis explicitly groups ZDB425, ZDB458 and ZDB464 and reports an estimated fitness effect of −5.4% with interval [−7.2%, −3.6%]. The canonical representation identifies a grouped intermediate-lineage estimate rather than treating the number as an individual-clone effect. The life-domain claim classification, attribution, neutral status and separate node identity are justified; no relationship direction or taxonomy is asserted.
decisions.limitations: The group estimate does not identify the causative genetic changes. ZDB425 and ZDB458 have private mutations, and the authors cannot exclude further changes along the main lineage between sampling points. The interval must not be generalized into a continuously measured effect across 10,000 generations.

decisions.rationale: Leon identifies ZDB19 and ZDB13 among the later fully potentiated pre-Cit+ lineage as early as 29,000 generations, reporting an overall +2.4% fitness estimate with 95% confidence interval [+1.4%, +3.4%]. The scope, label, classification as a life-domain claim, and neutral metadata preserve source meaning.
decisions.limitations: The pooled engineered-activation result does not demonstrate Cit+ cells already existed at generation 29,000, identify causative mutations, or guarantee evolutionary success.

decisions.rationale: Leon et al. identify ZDB19 and ZDB13 as members of a later fully potentiated pre-Cit+ group represented as early as 29,000 generations. They report a group fitness effect of +2.4%, with 95% confidence interval [+1.4%, +3.4%]. The candidate preserves the group-level estimate, time qualifier, biological lineage and distinction between engineered activation and historical Cit+ appearance. Kind, domain, identity, neutral metadata and standalone representation are supported.
decisions.limitations: The grouped estimate does not prove that Cit+ organisms were already present at generation 29,000, identify a specific potentiating mutation, or show that an initially beneficial mutant would inevitably establish in the evolving population.

decisions.rationale: The revised label correctly identifies the evolved generation-31,000 Ara−3 population, rather than the founding ancestor. Leon explicitly describes equally mixed engineered Cit+ and Cit− ZDB706 variants at about 1% combined frequency, a 0.9% Cit+ advantage and no support for the tested ecological-potentiation hypothesis. The attribution, scope, kind, life domain, neutral metadata and independent identity are justified.
decisions.limitations: P=0.053 for difference from pairwise competitions is marginal. The narrow experiment does not rule out all frequency-dependent or other ecological effects.

decisions.rationale: The revised canonical label correctly specifies an evolved generation-31,000 Ara−3 population mixture, not the ancestral founding population. Leon et al. report introducing equally mixed Cit+ and Cit− engineered ZDB706 variants at approximately 1% combined frequency into that evolved population and measuring a 0.9% Cit+ fitness advantage. The authors explicitly report no support for the ecological-potentiation hypothesis tested. Source identity, experimental population, comparison direction, life domain, claim kind and neutral metadata are preserved.
decisions.limitations: The difference from ordinary pairwise competition was marginal, with two-tailed P=0.053. A negative result in this particular mixture does not exclude other forms of ecological potentiation, frequency dependence or population interactions. The engineered variants were not the original founding strains. The revised candidate must be reviewed on its own merits rather than accepted because an earlier version was rejected.

decisions.rationale: Turner's retained source reports Cit−-specific PCR bands and phenotypic detection through 43,500 generations, without detection at 44,000 or later sampled time points. The node expressly says 'detectable', so it does not turn a screening result into proof of absolute extinction; its claim kind, life domain, source attribution and neutral metadata are justified.
decisions.limitations: PCR and phenotypic screening have detection limits, and the source does not reveal the precise instant or mechanism of lineage loss.

decisions.rationale: The retained Turner et al. (2015) source reports Cit−-specific PCR detection through 43,500 generations, no amplification from 44,000 generations onward, and matching phenotypic screening results in the sampled cultures. The candidate describes loss of detectable genotype and phenotype, not observation of every individual organism's disappearance. Its life-domain claim identity, bounded historical scope and neutral scientific metadata are justified.
decisions.limitations: Negative PCR and phenotypic screens are constrained by sampling and detection sensitivity. They do not establish an exact extinction time within the 500-generation interval or exclude an undetected residual Cit− population. No causal mechanism follows from disappearance alone.

decisions.rationale: The retained Turner passage states that Cit− persisted in all 20 replays started at generation 43,500 and all 20 at generation 40,000 after 500 generations, plus one 43,000-generation culture followed for 2,500 generations. Counts, timeframes, node identity and neutral reported status agree with the source.
decisions.limitations: The single extended culture is additional to the 40 short replays. Persistence in these replays does not establish survival under every possible prior environmental disturbance.

decisions.rationale: Turner et al. report Cit− persistence in all 20 independently propagated replays founded from generation 43,500 and all 20 controls founded from generation 40,000 after 500 generations. They separately report persistence in one generation-43,000 culture extended for 2,500 generations. The candidate preserves the three starting conditions, replicate counts, propagation durations and observed outcome. Claim kind, life domain, standalone identity and neutral metadata are justified.
decisions.limitations: The one extended replay is separate from the 40 shorter replays. Failure to reproduce extinction under standard conditions does not prove competitive extinction impossible or reproduce an unidentified historical laboratory perturbation. The candidate does not establish a universal survival guarantee.

decisions.rationale: Turner explicitly reports that a 43,000-generation Cit− clone invaded the 50,000-generation Ara−3 resident population and reached roughly 3 × 10^5 cells/mL, about tenfold below other treatments. The candidate preserves generation direction, measurement unit and the mean across high- and low-density starts. Kind, domain and neutral metadata are suitable.
decisions.limitations: The assay spans seven days, and invasion under these conditions does not show indefinite stable coexistence or resolve the earlier extinction.

decisions.rationale: The Turner source explicitly states that a generation-43,000 Cit− clone invaded a resident generation-50,000 population and reports a final mean Cit− density of approximately 3 × 10^5 cells/mL, about an order of magnitude below densities in the other treatments. The candidate preserves which population supplied the invading clone, which was the recipient, and the quantitative result. Life-domain claim identity, neutral metadata and independent representation are justified.
decisions.limitations: The measured density is the mean across high- and low-inoculum treatments in a short competition experiment. Successful reinvasion does not establish indefinite stable coexistence, an invariant ecological equilibrium or the cause of the original Cit− loss. The source does not justify reversing the invasion direction.

decisions.rationale: Turner explicitly states that the Cit− extinction cause remains unknown, rejects the authors' initial ongoing Cit+ adaptation explanation, and offers an unidentified rare random catastrophe as a proposed explanation. The node attributes the hypothesis, does not assert an observed catastrophe, and preserves the scoped historical uncertainty, life domain, kind and neutral metadata.
decisions.limitations: Proposed events such as residue or water issues were not observed. The evidence does not eliminate every possible ecological or fitness-related extinction mechanism.

decisions.rationale: Turner et al. explicitly state that the cause of Ara−3 Cit− lineage extinction remains unknown. They reject their initial ongoing-Cit+ adaptation explanation and propose a rare random catastrophe as a possible account, while acknowledging that its nature is unknown. The candidate clearly marks the perturbation as proposed rather than observed. The claim kind, life domain, historical attribution, neutral status, unresolved era, frontier=false and independent identity are justified.
decisions.limitations: The source does not demonstrate that a random catastrophe occurred, establish a particular laboratory error, or eliminate every conceivable fitness-mediated or ecological explanation. The rejection applies to the authors' original tested explanation, not all possible evolutionary models. No identity, taxonomy or graph relationship is independently established by this record.

support.quote: We analyze the performance of language models on two tasks that require identifying relevant information in their input contexts: multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval.

support.quote: To this end, we propose CoF (Coarse to Fine), a novel pipeline that utilizes off-the-shelf LLMs to automatically generate long-context QA instances with precise sentence-level citations, and leverage this pipeline to construct LongCite-45k, a large-scale SFT dataset for LQAC. Finally, we train LongCite-8B and LongCite-9B using the LongCite-45k dataset, successfully enabling their generation of accurate responses and fine-grained sentence-level citations in a single output.

canonical_record.label: JUNO 207-day atmospheric mass-splitting fits
canonical_record.summary: The September 2026 JUNO analysis reported 8,294 inverse-beta-decay candidates in 207.2 live days at an average 52.5 km reactor baseline and obtained different fitted atmospheric mass splittings under normal and inverted ordering using a Daya Bay constraint.

sources.title: Measurement of Neutrino Oscillation Parameters at JUNO and Indication of the Neutrino Mass Ordering

assertions.statement: The September 2026 JUNO analysis reported 8,294 inverse-beta-decay candidates in 207.2 live days at an average 52.5 km reactor baseline and obtained different fitted atmospheric mass splittings under normal and inverted ordering using a Daya Bay constraint.

scope.population: JUNO inverse-beta-decay candidate sample
scope.time: 207.2 live days, as reported in September 2026
scope.assumptions: The fitted atmospheric splitting is conditional on the chosen mass ordering and external Daya Bay constraint; the sample is not an independent determination of ordering.
scope.uncertainty: Oscillation-parameter fits and event counts do not establish the absolute neutrino mass or conclusive ordering.

support.quote: The analysis is based on 207.2 live days of data, comprising 8,294 inverse beta-decay candidates collected at an average reactor baseline of 52.5 km. A world-leading precision of approximately 1% was achieved for the atmospheric neutrino mass splitting $\Delta m^2_{31}$, with $\Delta m^2_{31}=+2.509^{+0.027}_{-0.025}\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV}^2$ for normal ordering and $\Delta m^2_{31}=-2.482^{+0.025}_{-0.026}\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV}^2$ for inverted ordering, using the Daya Bay constraint in the fit to resolve the correct physical minimum under each mass-ordering hypothesis.

canonical_record.label: KATRIN effective electron-antineutrino mass bound
canonical_record.summary: KATRIN reported a fitted squared effective electron-antineutrino mass of -0.14 (+0.13/-0.15) eV² from five tritium beta-decay campaigns and an effective-mass upper limit of 0.45 eV at 90% confidence using 259 measurement days and 36 million electrons.

scope.assumptions: A negative unconstrained best-fit squared-mass parameter is a statistical fit result, not a physical negative neutrino mass; effective kinematic mass differs from the cosmological sum.

support.quote: Based on the first five neutrino-mass measurement campaigns, we derive a best-fit value of $m_\nu^{2} = {-0.14^{+0.13}_{-0.15}}~\mathrm{eV^2}$, resulting in an upper limit of $m_\nu < {0.45}~\mathrm{eV}$ at 90 % confidence level. With six times the statistics of previous data sets, amounting to 36 million electrons collected in 259 measurement days, a substantial reduction of the background level and improved systematic uncertainties, this result tightens KATRIN's previous bound by a factor of almost two.

scope.population: DESI DR2 BAO and external CMB combination
scope.assumptions: The two limits are conditional on alternative cosmological dark-energy parametrizations; not BAO-only data.
scope.uncertainty: Neither 95% upper limit is a direct mass observation or a universal model-independent upper bound.
scope.quantifiers: 0.064 eV (ΛCDM) and 0.16 eV (w0wa)

support.quote: From the combination of DESI and CMB we derive 95% upper limits on the sum of neutrino masses, finding $\sum m_\nu<0.064$ eV assuming $\Lambda$CDM and $\sum m_\nu<0.16$ eV in the $w_0w_a$ model.

canonical_record.label: DESI DR2 neutrino mass tension and boundary-sensitive inference
canonical_record.summary: The DESI DR2 neutrino-constraints analysis reported a Feldman-Cousins 95% bound Σmν<0.053 eV after correcting for the zero-mass boundary, below the oscillation-inferred lower limit, and a separate effective-mass parametrization yielding 3σ tension under its analysis assumptions.

sources.title: Constraints on Neutrino Physics from DESI DR2 BAO and DR1 Full Shape

assertions.statement: The DESI DR2 neutrino-constraints analysis reported a Feldman-Cousins 95% bound Σmν<0.053 eV after correcting for the zero-mass boundary, below the oscillation-inferred lower limit, and a separate effective-mass parametrization yielding 3σ tension under its analysis assumptions.

scope.population: DESI DR2 BAO combined with external Planck and ACT CMB datasets as analyzed in this study
scope.assumptions: Feldman-Cousins and Bayesian effective-parameter results are distinct statistical constructions; effective negative density is an analysis device, not physical negative neutrino mass.
scope.uncertainty: Claimed tension depends on model assumptions, priors and treatment of boundaries; source itself mentions possible systematics and evolving dark energy.
scope.quantifiers: Σmν<0.053 eV (95% Feldman-Cousins); 3σ effective-parameter tension

support.quote: However, we determine using frequentist and Bayesian methods that our constraints are in tension with the lower limits derived from neutrino oscillations. Correcting for the physical boundary at zero mass, we report a 95% Feldman-Cousins upper limit of $\sum m_\nu<0.053$ eV, breaching the lower limit from neutrino oscillations. Considering a more general Bayesian analysis with an effective cosmological neutrino mass parameter, $\sum m_{\nu,\rm{eff}}$, that allows for negative energy densities and removes unsatisfactory prior weight effects, we derive constraints that are in $3\sigma$ tension with the same oscillation limit.

canonical_record.label: Planck 2018 BAO mass bounds change under hierarchy priors
canonical_record.summary: A Bayesian reanalysis using Planck 2018 CMB plus BOSS DR12, MGS and 6dFGS BAO data reported 95%-confidence neutrino mass-sum limits of 0.12 eV (degenerate masses), 0.15 eV (normal ordering) and 0.17 eV (inverted ordering), attributing their differences to mass-sum priors.

canonical_record.label: DESI and CMB neutrino constraints with isocurvature allowed
canonical_record.summary: A 2026 joint CMB, DESI DR2 and supernova analysis reported that allowing a neutrino-density isocurvature mode shifted its 95% neutrino mass-sum limits from 0.052 to 0.057 eV under ΛCDM and 0.111 to 0.115 eV under dynamical dark energy, without detecting the isocurvature mode.

scope.time: 2026 paper under two cosmological model assumptions
scope.assumptions: The comparison changes initial-condition assumptions within each dark-energy model; these are model/prior-dependent posterior limits.
scope.uncertainty: The sub-oscillation-minimum ΛCDM bound can arise from a prior extending to zero and is not a model-independent exclusion of normal ordering.

support.quote: Within the $\Lambda$CDM model, the 95\% upper limit weakens only marginally from $\sum m_\nu < 0.052$ eV (purely adiabatic) to $< 0.057$ eV (including NDI), with the NDI amplitude consistent with zero. In the CPL dynamical dark energy model, the adiabatic limit is $< 0.111$ eV, shifting to $< 0.115$ eV with NDI, yet the isocurvature mode remains undetected.

canonical_record.label: Hierarchy-aware prior relaxes cosmological mass-sum bound
canonical_record.summary: The 2026 cosmological isocurvature analysis reported that its purely adiabatic ΛCDM upper limit of 0.052 eV lay below the oscillation-implied normal-ordering minimum of 0.05878 eV because of a statistical prior extending to zero, while a hierarchy-informed prior raised the reported upper limit to 0.092 eV.

scope.population: Joint CMB-SPA, DESI DR2 BAO and DES Year 5 supernova analysis
scope.time: 2026 paper, comparing alternative neutrino mass-sum priors
scope.assumptions: The 0.052 eV bound is conditional on an unconstrained-from-below-by-oscillation mass prior; the 0.092 eV bound reflects a hierarchy-informed prior.
scope.uncertainty: The paper's prior analysis does not show that the mass sum is physically negative or establish neutrino hierarchy from cosmology.
scope.quantifiers: initial 95% limit 0.052 eV, oscillation floor 0.05878 eV, revised 95% upper limit 0.092 eV

support.quote: Notably, the adiabatic $\Lambda$CDM limit of $0.052$ eV lies below the minimum sum required by the normal neutrino mass hierarchy ($0.05878$ eV), indicating that this bound is an artifact of the statistical prior extending to zero. Imposing a physically motivated hierarchy-informed prior raises the limit to $< 0.092$ eV. Our results demonstrate that current data show no evidence for NDI modes and that the inferred neutrino mass upper limit is robust against this extension, but a definitive, model-independent bound requires addressing prior dependencies and dark energy uncertainties.

canonical_record.label: Kurvers spatial producer-scrounger evolutionary simulation
canonical_record.summary: Kurvers and colleagues modeled group foraging with a spatially explicit genetic algorithm whose simulated agents could alternate between producing and scrounging; the exploration level and the probability of scrounging were distinct, evolving continuous traits each ranging from 0 to 1.

assertions.statement: Kurvers and colleagues modeled group foraging with a spatially explicit genetic algorithm whose simulated agents could alternate between producing and scrounging; the exploration level and the probability of scrounging were distinct, evolving continuous traits each ranging from 0 to 1.

scope.population: Simulated agents in a spatial producer-scrounger foraging game
scope.time: 2012 publication; tactics alternated within foraging rounds and genetic traits evolved across rounds
scope.assumptions: Exploration is a level or score affecting spatial movement and social attraction, not itself defined as the probability of exploring; scrounging probability governs tactic selection.
scope.uncertainty: Computational model rather than direct animal observation; outcomes depend on implemented spatial and selection assumptions.

support.quote:
Here we incorporated travel times for scroungers and allowed individuals to play a mixed strategy by alternating between producer and scrounger within rounds. Importantly, we did not start with
a priori
differences between individuals by introducing fast and slow explorers in the model, or by assigning fixed foraging strategies (either producing, or scrounging) to individuals. Both the level of exploration and the scrounging probability were on a continuous scale (0–1) and were allowed to evolve (i.e., not fixed).

An individual’s strategy was encoded in a 2-locus real-valued chromosome, with locus 1 coding for the probability of scrounging P
S_I
and locus 2 coding for the value of exploration E
I
. Both loci ranged from 0 to 1

Exploration level and scrounging probability are different evolving continuous variables on the interval 0–1; a two-locus real-valued simulation chromosome encodes them separately. Both supplied support excerpts match their exact Unicode offsets and are unique. The canonical record equals the proposed model node, and the assertion statement equals its summary. The title, source identity, kind=model and domain=social accurately characterize a simulation of social foraging. Status=reported, era=undated and frontier=false carry only their stipulated neutral meanings. decisions.limitations: The 'chromosome' is a genetic-algorithm representation, not an experimentally observed animal genome. Exploration is a continuous movement/social-attraction trait, not an independent probability of choosing to explore; only scrounging is directly specified as tactic-choice probability. The results depend on simulation rules for spatial movement, food distribution, predators, detection, reproduction and parameter settings. They do not independently validate behavior in wild animals or a universal evolutionary equilibrium.

support.quote: Metallic, oxygen-deficient compounds in the Ba-La-Cu-O system, with the composition BaxLa5-xCu5O5(3-y) have been prepared in polycrystalline form. Samples with x=1 and 0.75, y>0, annealed below 900°C under reducing conditions, consist of three phases, one of them a perovskite-like mixed-valent copper compound. Upon cooling, the samples show a linear decrease in resistivity, then an approximately logarithmic increase, interpreted as a beginning of localization. Finally an abrupt decrease by up to three orders of magnitude occurs, reminiscent of the onset of percolative superconductivity. The highest onset temperature is observed in the 30 K range. It is markedly reduced by high current densities. Thus, it results partially from the percolative nature, bute possibly also from 2 D superconducting fluctuations of double perovskite layers of one of the phases present. © 1986 Springer-Verlag.
